The parties met at the property, discussed the scope of work, and signed a one-page handwritten document. That writing listed the address, identified certain tasks—replacement of drywall, repainting, and flooring repair—and stated a total price of $18,500. It also noted that work would begin “next week.” Plaintiff paid Defendant a $9,000 deposit. Defendant thereafter performed limited demolition but did not complete the repairs. When Plaintiff demanded completion or return of the deposit, Defendant asserted that the handwritten paper was merely an estimate and not a binding contract.

Plaintiff sued for breach of contract and restitution. After a bench trial, the court now enters judgment.

**Legal Issue**

The principal issue is whether the handwritten agreement contained sufficiently definite terms and mutual assent to create an enforceable contract for home repairs.

**Applicable Law and Standard**

A valid contract requires offer, acceptance, consideration, and reasonably definite essential terms. A writing need not be formal or professionally drafted to be enforceable; handwritten agreements may bind the parties if the objective manifestations of assent show an intent to contract. In service contracts, essential terms generally include the identity of the parties, the subject matter, the price or method for determining price, and a sufficiently definite scope of performance. Where one party accepts payment and begins performance, that conduct may confirm the existence of a contract. Ambiguities are construed against the party who drafted the writing or seeks to avoid it after partial performance.

**Analysis**

The handwritten document here satisfies the minimum requirements for contract formation. It identified the parties, the property address, the repair categories to be completed, and a fixed total price. Although the phrase “next week” did not specify an exact start date, timing was not so indefinite as to defeat formation; the law commonly implies a reasonable time for performance where exact dates are omitted. Likewise, the absence of highly detailed construction specifications does not render the agreement unenforceable where the work categories were clear enough to permit performance and judicial enforcement.

Legal Issue
Whether the handwritten document constituted an enforceable contract for home repairs or an unenforceable agreement to agree lacking essential terms.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
To form a binding contract, there must be mutual assent to all material terms and consideration. A writing must be sufficiently definite to allow a court to determine the obligations and to fashion a remedy. Essential terms in a construction-services contract typically include the scope of work, price, timing for performance, and payment terms; where such terms are missing, courts may infer them only if industry custom or prior dealings supply a clear basis. Ambiguity is construed against formation where it reflects an absence of mutual assent. The burden rests on the party asserting contract formation.

Analysis
The notebook sheet described two general tasks and a total figure, but omitted key material terms. First, scope: “roof leak fix” and “replace gutters” are too indefinite to define performance obligations, warranty, methods, and materials beyond “materials included,” which itself is vague. The subsequent inspection revealed significant structural issues; the writing provides no mechanism for addressing latent conditions or change orders.

Second, time: “Work to start next week” lacks a definite commencement or completion date and provides no standard for timely performance. While courts may imply a reasonable time, the open-ended phrasing coupled with unresolved scope militates against enforceability.

Third, payment: There is no payment schedule, deposit term, or progress payment structure. In construction, the allocation of cash flow and milestones is material. Without it, a court cannot determine breach or damages tied to nonpayment or delay.

Fourth, mutual assent: The parties’ conduct—Defendant’s prompt statement that further agreement was needed after inspection—demonstrates that the writing reflected preliminary negotiations, contingent on a formal, more detailed contract. Plaintiff identifies no industry custom or prior course of dealing between these parties from which to supply the missing terms.

Plaintiff argues that the total price evidences agreement. But a price alone, without definite scope and timing, is insufficient in a construction context to establish enforceable obligations. The court declines to rewrite the parties’ bargain by supplying multiple material terms.

Conclusion
Because the handwritten document lacks essential terms and reflects no meeting of the minds, it did not create an enforceable contract. Judgment is entered for Defendant on the breach of contract claim. Any quasi-contract or quantum meruit claims are not before the Court on this motion and are not adjudicated herein. Contract interpretation is a question of law when the agreement is unambiguous. A borrower seeking to establish satisfaction of a debt bears the burden of showing compliance with the payment terms or a valid accord and satisfaction. Where a contract specifies the method, timing, and effect of payment, courts enforce those terms according to their plain meaning.

The agreement here is clear. It required timely monthly payments in a specified form and stated that only written confirmation from Lender would constitute acceptance of any payment as full satisfaction. This case arises from the sale of a used vehicle by the defendant, a private seller, to the plaintiff, the buyer. The plaintiff alleges that the defendant failed to disclose serious mechanical defects affecting the vehicle’s drivability and safety, including repeated transmission failure and prior flood damage. After the sale, the plaintiff discovered that the vehicle required extensive repairs and was substantially worth less than the purchase price. ### Background

The record shows that the defendant advertised the vehicle as “well maintained” and “ready to drive.” During negotiations, the plaintiff asked whether the car had any major mechanical problems or prior damage. The defendant responded that the vehicle was in “good condition” and did not disclose any known defects. Shortly after purchase, the plaintiff experienced transmission slippage and electrical failures. A mechanic later determined that the transmission had been previously repaired and was near complete failure, and that the vehicle showed signs of prior flood exposure.

The principal issue is whether a private seller of a used vehicle may be liable for failing to disclose known material defects when the buyer specifically inquires about the vehicle’s condition and the seller makes affirmative statements that omit or minimize those defects.

### Applicable Law and Standard of Review

A seller of personal property generally is not required to disclose every defect in an arm’s-length transaction. However, under common-law fraud and state consumer-protection principles, liability may arise where a seller knowingly conceals a material defect, makes a partial or misleading disclosure, or responds falsely to a direct inquiry. Materiality is established where the defect would likely affect the buyer’s decision to purchase or the price paid. We review the trial court’s factual findings for clear error and its legal conclusions de novo.

### Analysis

The trial court’s findings are supported by the record. The plaintiff asked direct questions about major defects and prior damage. The defendant’s statements that the vehicle was in “good condition” and “ready to drive” were not mere sales puffery in context; they were representations about the vehicle’s present condition. The evidence further showed that the defendant knew of the transmission problems and flood history before the sale. A seller who answers a buyer’s specific questions has a duty to speak truthfully and completely enough to avoid creating a misleading impression.

The defects were plainly material. A failing transmission and flood damage substantially affect both safety and value. The plaintiff relied on the defendant’s representations in completing the purchase, and that reliance was reasonable given the defendant’s superior knowledge of the vehicle’s history.

### Conclusion

Because the defendant knowingly failed to disclose material defects and made misleading statements in response to the plaintiff’s inquiries, the judgment of the trial court is affirmed. The plaintiff is entitled to rescission or, if rescission is impracticable, damages measured by the difference between the vehicle’s represented value and its actual condition at the time of sale.

Whether Tenant lawfully withheld rent for December 2022 and January 2023 based on alleged habitability problems, thereby excusing payment under applicable landlord-tenant law.

Standard of Review
The Court reviews the parties’ stipulated facts and admissible declarations for summary judgment purposes, applying state landlord-tenant principles governing the implied warranty of habitability and tenant remedies. Questions of law are reviewed de novo; undisputed factual inferences are viewed in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party.

Applicable Law
Most jurisdictions recognize an implied warranty of habitability requiring landlords to maintain premises in a condition fit for basic human habitation. Remedies for breach typically include repair and deduct, withholding rent in escrow, or terminating the lease when conditions are severe and unremedied. Tenants who withhold rent must generally provide notice, allow reasonable time for repair, and not unilaterally abrogate payment absent persistent, substantial defects. The record shows Tenant notified Landlord of defects on October 5, 2022, and again on October 20. Tenant continued to occupy the premises during the months in question and did not vacate or seek court relief prior to withholding rent.

Landlord disputes the severity and timing of the alleged conditions and asserts Tenant failed to follow statutory procedures for rent withholding. The trial was conducted on stipulated exhibits and testimony from Tenant, Landlord’s property manager, and a maintenance contractor.

Legal Issue
Whether Tenant lawfully withheld rent under the state’s implied warranty of habitability and rent-withholding statutes and regulations, thereby precluding Landlord from recovering unpaid rent and late fees.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
The implied warranty of habitability requires landlords to maintain rental premises in a condition fit for human habitation. Material breaches—such as lack of heat, pervasive infestations, or unremedied plumbing leaks—may justify rent withholding or repair-and-deduct remedies when authorized by statute. To lawfully withhold rent, tenants must: (1) provide reasonable notice of the defective conditions; (2) allow a reasonable opportunity to cure; (3) place withheld sums into escrow if required; and (4) limit withholding to a reasonable abatement proportionate to the defect. The tenant bears the burden to establish both materiality of the conditions and compliance with procedural requirements.

Analysis
Tenant testified that heat was “off and on” during January and February, that roaches were “often seen” in the kitchen, and that a bathroom leak persisted for “weeks.” However, Tenant’s written notices consist of two text messages to the property manager on January 5 and January 20 referencing “cold apartment” and “bugs,” without dates, photos, or corroboration. Landlord produced service logs and vendor invoices showing a same-day pilot relight on January 6, a thermostat replacement on January 21, and professional pest treatment on January 23 and February 6. The maintenance contractor testified credibly that the bathroom leak reported February 10 was repaired within 48 hours, with no further work orders.

Even assuming some temporary disruption, the record does not establish a sustained, material deprivation of essential services. More critically, Tenant did not comply with statutory procedures: she did not provide a formal written notice specifying defects and a deadline to cure; she withheld the entirety of two months’ rent rather than a reasonable abatement; and she did not place the withheld sums in escrow as required. Tenant admitted on cross-examination that she retained the funds for other expenses. The absence of escrow and the wholesale nonpayment weigh heavily against lawful withholding. Landlord’s documented remedial efforts within days of notice further undercut any claim of uncured material breach.

Conclusion
Tenant failed to prove that the premises were rendered uninhabitable or that she complied with the statutory prerequisites for rent withholding. Judgment is entered for Defendant Oak Properties, LLC, for the unpaid rent and contractual late fees, less any amounts already tendered, with costs. This ruling is without prejudice to Tenant’s ability to seek prospective relief should future material defects arise and statutory procedures be followed.

Approximately six weeks later, Defendant sent Plaintiff an email stating that the full deposit had been retained for “cleaning, repainting, and general repairs.”

Plaintiff filed this action, alleging that Defendant improperly withheld the deposit because no timely itemized statement was provided and because the claimed deductions reflected ordinary wear and tear rather than tenant-caused damage. Security deposits are governed by statute and are strictly regulated. In general, a landlord may withhold amounts only for unpaid rent, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, or other charges expressly authorized by the lease. Most statutes further require the landlord, within a specified period after surrender of the premises, to return the deposit or provide a written, itemized statement of deductions. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may forfeit the landlord’s right to retain the deposit. The plaintiff bears the burden of showing payment of the deposit and surrender of possession; the landlord bears the burden of proving lawful deductions.

Plaintiff established that the deposit was paid, that the tenancy ended, and that possession was surrendered with a forwarding address provided. The burden therefore shifted to Defendant to justify withholding the funds. Defendant did not do so.

A landlord may not shift the routine costs of preparing a unit for a new tenant onto the departing tenant absent proof of excessive damage.

Plaintiff, startled, stepped backward off the curb, lost footing, and fell, sustaining a fractured wrist. Plaintiff alleges Defendant is liable for failure to leash the dog and to control an animal with dangerous propensities. Defendant contends the dog had no known vicious tendencies, did not bite or touch Plaintiff, and that any local leash ordinance does not impose strict civil liability in the absence of proximate causation or negligence.

Legal Issue
Whether Defendant is liable for Plaintiff’s injuries where the dog was unleashed but did not physically contact Plaintiff, and there is no evidence of known dangerous propensities, under negligence or strict liability theories.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
A plaintiff asserting strict liability for injuries caused by a domestic animal must show the owner knew or should have known of the animal’s dangerous propensities. Negligence requires proof of duty, breach, causation, and damages. Violation of a safety ordinance, such as a leash law, may constitute negligence per se if the statute was designed to protect against the type of harm suffered and the violation proximately caused the injury. Proximate cause requires a sufficiently direct causal connection between the breach and the injury.

Analysis
There is no evidence the dog exhibited prior aggressive behavior or that Defendant knew of any dangerous propensity. The record reflects the dog neither lunged nor made contact, and no growling or snapping occurred. Accordingly, strict liability is not established.

On negligence, Plaintiff argues Defendant breached a duty by failing to use a leash, citing a municipal ordinance requiring dogs to be restrained on public ways. Even assuming the ordinance applies to the location of the incident and its violation constitutes negligence per se, Plaintiff must still establish proximate causation. The undisputed evidence shows Plaintiff fell after stepping off the curb in reaction to the dog’s presence, not due to any physical interference or aggressive act by the animal. A generalized startle response, without more, is too attenuated to constitute proximate cause where the dog’s behavior was non-threatening and typical. Defendant maintained verbal control; the dog heeded commands and remained within a few feet. The chain of events culminating in Plaintiff’s misstep off the curb amounts to an intervening reaction not proximately caused by Defendant’s conduct.

Because Plaintiff has not established strict liability or proximate causation under negligence or negligence per se, judgment is entered for Defendant. The complaint is dismissed with prejudice. Each party shall bear its own costs.

The principal issue is whether Defendant may be held liable for Plaintiff’s injuries where an unleashed dog caused Plaintiff to react and fall, but the evidence does not establish prior dangerous propensities or negligent handling by Defendant.

A pet owner may be liable under either strict liability, where an owner knows or should know of an animal’s dangerous propensities, or ordinary negligence, where the owner fails to exercise reasonable care in controlling the animal. Defendant testified, credibly and without contradiction, that the dog was leashed immediately before the event and that the collar failed unexpectedly. Plaintiff fell while stepping backward on uneven pavement; the dog neither touched nor threatened her in a manner that would make the precise injury reasonably foreseeable. While the event was unfortunate, tort law does not impose liability for every injury occurring in the vicinity of an animal.

Because Plaintiff failed to prove dangerous propensity, negligent restraint, or legally sufficient causation, judgment shall be entered in favor of Defendant. Plaintiff’s complaint is dismissed with prejudice.

**IN THE COURT OF COMMON PLEAS**

**Opinion and Order**

This matter concerns a dispute between the plaintiff, the lender of a personal item, and the defendant, the borrower, over whether the item was returned in damaged condition and, if so, whether the defendant is legally responsible for that damage. After a bench trial, the Court enters judgment for the defendant.

### Background

The plaintiff testified that she lent the defendant a vintage acoustic guitar for use during a weekend performance. The parties agree that the guitar was delivered in playable condition and returned three days later. The plaintiff contends that, upon return, the guitar exhibited a crack near the bridge and diminished sound quality, requiring repair. She seeks damages equal to the repair estimate and alleged loss in value.

The defendant acknowledges borrowing the guitar but denies causing any damage. He testified that he transported the instrument in the hard case provided by the plaintiff, used it only indoors, and returned it in the same condition in which he received it. He further presented testimony from a guitar technician who inspected the instrument after the dispute arose and opined that the crack was consistent with age-related wood separation and humidity fluctuation rather than recent impact or misuse.

### Legal Issue

The principal issue is whether the plaintiff proved, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the defendant returned the borrowed item in a damaged condition caused by his failure to exercise reasonable care.

### Applicable Law and Standard of Review

A bailment for the mutual benefit or accommodation of the parties imposes on the borrower a duty of ordinary care. To recover, the plaintiff must establish delivery of the property in good condition, return in damaged condition, and a causal connection between the damage and the defendant’s breach of that duty. While proof that property was returned damaged may permit an inference of negligence in some circumstances, that inference may be rebutted by credible evidence showing reasonable care or an alternative cause.

### Analysis

The plaintiff established that the guitar was lent to the defendant and later returned. However, the evidence does not persuasively establish that the complained-of condition was caused during the borrowing period or by negligent handling. The plaintiff offered photographs taken after return and a repair estimate, but no contemporaneous photographs or expert testimony showing the guitar’s precise condition immediately before the loan. The repair estimate identifies the existence of a crack but does not attribute it to any particular event.

By contrast, the defendant’s testimony regarding storage, transport, and use was consistent and unrebutted. More importantly, the technician’s testimony provided a plausible non-negligent explanation: that the separation likely developed from preexisting structural stress and environmental conditions common in older wooden instruments. The Court finds that testimony credible. On this record, the plaintiff has not shown that the damage more likely than not resulted from the defendant’s conduct rather than ordinary wear, latent weakness, or natural deterioration.

### Conclusion

Because the plaintiff failed to carry the burden of proving negligence and causation, judgment is entered **for the defendant**. The plaintiff’s claim is dismissed with prejudice.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT OF RIVERVIEW COUNTY

Smith v. Johnson

Background
Plaintiff Daniel Smith and Defendant Laura Johnson collaborated to develop and sell a software product in 2022. Smith contributed coding, product design, and customer support; Johnson contributed capital for hosting and marketing, and she managed invoicing under her existing LLC. The parties did not execute a written partnership agreement. Smith alleges that, during meetings in March and April 2022, Johnson verbally agreed that they would split net profits from the product equally. The product launched in May 2022 and yielded substantial revenue by year’s end. Johnson paid Smith a flat monthly amount she characterized as a “contractor stipend,” but did not remit any share of profits. Smith brought suit for breach of an oral partnership agreement and, in the alternative, unjust enrichment. Johnson denies any partnership or profit-sharing promise and argues the alleged oral agreement is unenforceable under the statute of frauds.

Legal Issue
Whether an oral promise to share business profits between co-venturers is enforceable and, if so, whether the evidence establishes an agreement entitling Smith to a share of profits.

Applicable Law/Standard of Review
Partnerships may be formed by oral agreement where the parties intend to carry on as co-owners of a business for profit. Sharing of profits is prima facie evidence of a partnership unless received in payment of wages or debt. The statute of frauds does not bar oral agreements capable of being performed within one year or those not involving a transfer of an interest in real property. Even absent an enforceable contract, equity may provide restitution to prevent unjust enrichment when one party confers a benefit under circumstances that make retention inequitable.

Analysis
The record demonstrates a meeting of the minds sufficient to form an oral partnership agreement. Smith’s testimony that the parties agreed to split profits 50/50 is corroborated by contemporaneous emails from April 5 and April 12, 2022, in which Johnson refers to “our launch” and “splitting profits after expenses.” Johnson’s subsequent conduct—granting Smith administrative access, joint decision-making on pricing, and listing both names on pitch materials—supports an intent to co-own the venture for profit.

Johnson’s argument that payments to Smith were mere contractor wages is unpersuasive. The flat monthly payments do not negate a separate entitlement to profits; moreover, Johnson’s own messages distinguished the stipend as an “advance until profits are distributed.” The profit-sharing arrangement was capable of performance within one year because the product launched and generated revenue within months. The statute of frauds therefore does not bar enforcement. Nor does the absence of a written partnership agreement defeat formation where conduct and profit-sharing intent are established.

Even if the Court were to find no enforceable partnership, the alternative claim for unjust enrichment would warrant restitution given Smith’s substantial, non-gratuitous contributions directly producing the revenue Johnson retained. But the evidence supports a contractual relationship: an oral partnership with a 50/50 net profit split after documented expenses.

Conclusion
The Court finds an enforceable oral partnership agreement existed between Smith and Johnson to share net profits equally. Johnson breached that agreement by failing to remit Smith’s 50% share. Judgment is entered for Plaintiff. Within thirty days, the parties shall exchange an accounting of revenues and legitimate expenses for the product from May 1, 2022, through December 31, 2023. Upon that accounting, Defendant shall pay Plaintiff 50% of net profits for that period, plus prejudgment interest as allowed by law. Plaintiff’s unjust enrichment claim is dismissed as duplicative.

Smith, Plaintiff,
v.
Dawson, Defendant.

Opinion and Order

Background
Plaintiff James Smith and Defendant Laura Dawson collaborated to launch a specialty coffee roasting venture in 2022. Smith contributed $50,000 in startup capital, secured a supplier contract, and undertook marketing and distribution. Dawson managed day-to-day operations and production. Smith alleges that before launching, the parties had an oral agreement that net profits would be shared equally. For the first year, Dawson periodically reported profit figures and transmitted three equal distributions to Smith. In mid-2023, Dawson ceased making distributions, asserting there was no enforceable agreement and that any prior transfers were discretionary bonuses. Smith brought this action for breach of contract and, in the alternative, unjust enrichment. Dawson denies the existence of a binding agreement and invokes the statute of frauds.

Legal Issue
Whether an oral promise to share business profits, supported by mutual consideration and sufficiently definite terms, is enforceable, and whether the statute of frauds bars enforcement.

Applicable Law/Standard of Review
To prove breach of contract, a plaintiff must show offer, acceptance, consideration, and sufficiently definite terms to ascertain obligations and provide a remedy. Oral contracts are generally enforceable unless a statute requires a writing. The statute of frauds typically requires writings for contracts that cannot be performed within one year or involve interests in real property. An agreement of indefinite duration is outside the one-year provision if it could be fully performed within a year. Partial performance and course of dealing may evidence contract terms. In the absence of an enforceable contract, a party may recover in unjust enrichment to prevent retention of benefits conferred under inequitable circumstances.

Analysis
The record establishes mutual assent and consideration. Smith contributed capital and supplier access; Dawson contributed labor and operational control. The parties discussed and agreed to split net profits equally. The course of performance—three equal profit distributions and contemporaneous profit reports—corroborates the agreement’s existence and terms. Dawson’s characterization of those payments as bonuses is unsupported by any contemporaneous documentation and is inconsistent with equal, periodic distributions tethered to stated profit figures.

The terms are sufficiently definite: “net profits” commonly refer to revenues minus ordinary and necessary business expenses, a standard accounting concept for small enterprises. Courts regularly enforce profit-sharing arrangements defined in those terms, particularly where, as here, the parties’ performance supplies context.

The statute of frauds does not bar enforcement. The agreement had no fixed term and could be fully performed within one year if the venture ceased operations or the parties wound up affairs. Indefinite-duration agreements are not within the one-year provision. Additionally, Smith’s substantial performance—capital infusion and ongoing services—further removes the agreement from strict application of the statute.

Even were there any defect in contract formation, equity would compel restitution. Smith’s capital and efforts conferred a measurable benefit on the venture; Dawson’s unilateral cessation of distributions while retaining profits would unjustly enrich her.

Conclusion
The Court finds an enforceable oral contract to share net profits equally. Defendant breached that agreement by withholding Smith’s share after mid-2023. Judgment is entered for Plaintiff on the breach of contract claim. Plaintiff is entitled to an accounting of net profits from July 1, 2023 to present and payment of fifty percent of those profits, together with prejudgment interest as provided by statute. The unjust enrichment claim is denied as moot. An order for accounting will issue forthwith.

Plaintiff, a business partner in a small retail venture, brought this action against defendant, his co-partner, alleging that defendant orally promised to share future business profits equally and later failed to do so. Plaintiff contends that the promise created an enforceable agreement requiring defendant to remit a portion of the venture’s earnings. Defendant denies that any binding profit-sharing contract existed and argues that, at most, the parties discussed a preliminary business arrangement that was never reduced to writing or made sufficiently definite.

### Background

The record shows that the parties met several times to discuss opening and operating a neighborhood specialty store. Plaintiff contributed labor and some start-up assistance; defendant supplied the premises and initial inventory. During these discussions, the parties allegedly agreed that profits would be split evenly. No written partnership agreement was executed. The business operated for several months, after which defendant retained the earnings and excluded plaintiff from further distributions. Plaintiff then filed suit seeking enforcement of the alleged oral promise.

### Legal Issue

The central issue is whether an oral promise to share business profits is enforceable where the parties never executed a written agreement and the evidence does not establish a definite, complete contract.

### Applicable Law and Standard of Review

Under general contract principles, an agreement is enforceable only if the parties manifested mutual assent to sufficiently definite terms. Courts may enforce oral agreements in some commercial settings, but where the alleged arrangement concerns an ongoing business relationship, the plaintiff must prove the essential terms with reasonable certainty. If the agreement is too indefinite, or if the parties intended to negotiate and memorialize their arrangement later, no binding contract arises. On review of the trial court’s findings, the court examines legal conclusions de novo and factual findings for clear error.

### Analysis

Plaintiff’s claim fails because the evidence does not establish an enforceable oral contract with the requisite certainty. Although the parties discussed sharing profits, the record leaves unresolved several material terms: the duration of the arrangement, the scope of each party’s duties, how losses would be allocated, whether expenses would be deducted before distribution, and what accounting method would govern. These are not minor details; they are core terms of a business profit-sharing agreement.

The evidence also supports defendant’s position that the discussions were preliminary. The parties never signed a partnership agreement, never opened a joint account, and never adopted a formal accounting structure. Plaintiff’s own testimony indicates that the parties expected to “work out the details later,” which is inconsistent with an immediate, binding commitment. Courts do not create contracts for parties where essential terms remain open.

Plaintiff’s reliance on partial performance does not alter the result. While performance may sometimes corroborate an agreement, it cannot supply the missing essential terms necessary to form one. The record shows only that plaintiff assisted in the business during its early stages; that conduct is equally consistent with an informal business collaboration that never matured into an enforceable profit-sharing contract.

### Conclusion

Because plaintiff failed to prove the existence of a definite and enforceable oral agreement to share profits, judgment is entered for defendant. The trial court’s dismissal is affirmed.

The evidence at trial showed that Plaintiff and Defendant collaborated for several months in developing client leads and preparing proposals for a new consulting business. Plaintiff testified that, during several informal conversations, Defendant stated that “we’ll split the profits” once the business became successful. Plaintiff thereafter contributed time, introduced prospective clients, and assisted with preliminary operations. To establish an enforceable oral contract, a plaintiff must prove offer, acceptance, consideration, and sufficiently definite essential terms. Courts may enforce oral agreements in commercial settings, but only where the parties’ obligations can be determined with reasonable certainty. A promise that is indefinite as to material terms is not enforceable. Likewise, while profit sharing may be evidence of a partnership, it is not conclusive absent proof of mutual intent to form a partnership and agreement on the essential incidents of that relationship.

Plaintiff did not carry his burden of proving an enforceable agreement. The phrase “we’ll split the profits,” as described in the testimony, is too indefinite on this record to establish a binding contract. The parties never agreed on what constituted “profits,” whether expenses, salaries, or capital reimbursements would be deducted first, when distributions would occur, how losses would be allocated, or whether either party could withdraw from the venture. The surrounding conduct also undermines Plaintiff’s claim. Plaintiff’s contributions of labor and contacts may support compensation for services rendered, but they do not, without more, establish a contractual right to half of all business profits.

**Background**

Plaintiff, a former partner in a small equipment-rental venture, brings this action against Defendant, the business associate with whom Plaintiff operated the business for approximately four years. The parties did not execute a comprehensive written partnership agreement, but they jointly purchased inventory, maintained a shared business account, and divided profits equally. After their relationship deteriorated, the business ceased operations. Plaintiff alleges that Defendant took possession of several items of business equipment, withdrew funds from the shared account, and refused repeated demands to account for or return Plaintiff’s share of the assets. Defendant contends the retained property represented compensation for unpaid labor and that the remaining funds were used to satisfy business debts.

Following a bench trial, the Court makes findings of fact and conclusions of law.

**Legal Issues**

The principal issue is whether Defendant wrongfully retained shared business assets after dissolution of the parties’ partnership. Relatedly, the Court must determine whether Defendant met any burden to justify unilateral possession of partnership property or offset Plaintiff’s share based on alleged unpaid compensation.

**Applicable Law and Standard of Review**

In the absence of a contrary agreement, general partnership principles govern. Property acquired with partnership funds and used for partnership purposes is presumed to be partnership property. Upon dissolution, each partner owes the other fiduciary duties of loyalty, candor, and accounting. A partner may not unilaterally appropriate partnership assets for personal benefit without consent or a proper accounting. Where one partner retains control of partnership property, that partner bears the burden to provide a reliable accounting of assets, liabilities, and any claimed offsets.

Because this matter was tried to the Court, factual findings are based on the preponderance of the evidence.

**Analysis**

The evidence establishes that the disputed equipment was purchased from the shared business account and listed on the venture’s tax filings as business assets. Defendant does not dispute possession of that equipment after dissolution. Nor does Defendant dispute withdrawing the remaining account balance shortly before closing the account. These facts create a straightforward presumption that the property and funds were partnership assets subject to equal distribution after payment of legitimate business obligations.

Defendant’s justification is insufficient. Although Defendant testified that Plaintiff owed compensation for extra labor, Defendant produced no contemporaneous records, invoices, wage agreement, or written amendment to the parties’ profit-sharing arrangement. A partner’s claim for additional compensation is not presumed and must be supported by agreement or competent proof. Likewise, Defendant offered only generalized testimony regarding alleged debts, without bank records, receipts, or creditor statements tying the withdrawals to partnership liabilities.

By contrast, Plaintiff introduced account statements, purchase records, and written demands for an accounting that went unanswered. Defendant’s refusal to provide records, coupled with continued exclusive possession of the equipment, breached the duty to account and supports the inference of wrongful retention.

**Conclusion**

Judgment is entered for Plaintiff. The Court finds that Defendant wrongfully retained partnership assets and failed to establish any lawful offset. Plaintiff is entitled to an accounting, return of one-half of the net value of the retained equipment and withdrawn funds after proven business debts, and such further relief as necessary to effectuate distribution. The parties shall submit a proposed accounting schedule within 21 days.

Defendant contends that he was entitled to keep the assets because he had managed the business operations and incurred expenses on behalf of the venture.

### Background

Although they did not execute a detailed written partnership agreement, the record shows that both contributed capital, shared profits, and jointly purchased business property used in the enterprise. When the relationship deteriorated, Plaintiff requested an accounting and return of the business assets. Defendant refused, asserting that he had exclusive control over the property and that Plaintiff had abandoned the business.

### Legal Issue

### Applicable Law and Standard of Review

Under general partnership principles, partners owe one another duties of loyalty, care, and full accounting with respect to partnership property. Absent an agreement to the contrary, partnership assets are owned by the partnership and must be distributed according to each partner’s interest upon dissolution. A partner in possession of partnership property may not unilaterally appropriate it for personal use or refuse to account for proceeds derived from it.

In reviewing the evidence, the court considers whether Plaintiff proved by a preponderance of the evidence that the assets were partnership property and that Defendant retained them without lawful justification.

### Analysis

The evidence supports Plaintiff’s claim. Bank records, purchase invoices, and testimony from third-party vendors establish that the disputed equipment and inventory were acquired with partnership funds and used in the ordinary course of the business. Nor did he produce a credible accounting showing that the retained property was offset by unpaid expenses or advances sufficient to justify exclusive possession.

Defendant’s argument that Plaintiff “abandoned” the business is unpersuasive. Even if Plaintiff ceased active participation, abandonment does not extinguish a partner’s ownership interest absent a formal dissolution and accounting. The record shows that Plaintiff repeatedly demanded access to the books and return of the property, which is inconsistent with any intent to relinquish his interest.

Because Defendant retained partnership assets without consent and failed to account for them, his conduct was inconsistent with the duties owed between partners. Plaintiff is therefore entitled to recovery of the property or, if return is impracticable, its proven value.

For the foregoing reasons, judgment is entered in favor of Plaintiff. Defendant wrongfully retained shared business assets and must return them or compensate Plaintiff for their value, together with an accounting consistent with this opinion.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT OF WYANDOTTE COUNTY

Former Partner, Plaintiff,
v.
Business Associate, Defendant.

OPINION AND ORDER

Background
Plaintiff and Defendant operated a small logistics venture as equal members of an LLC formed in 2019. In 2022, the parties executed a written Operating Agreement providing that company assets—including trucks, accounts receivable, and customer lists—were the property of the LLC; that members owed fiduciary duties to the company; and that a withdrawing member would be paid the fair value of his membership interest as determined under a book-value formula following an accounting. In 2023, Plaintiff ceased working for the venture after a dispute over expansion plans, notified vendors he was “no longer involved,” and demanded that Defendant transfer to him two trucks and certain receivables he characterized as “joint property.” Defendant refused, continued operating the LLC, and offered to commence the contractually mandated valuation process. Plaintiff filed this action for conversion and breach of fiduciary duty, alleging Defendant wrongfully retained “shared business assets.”

Legal Issue
Whether Defendant wrongfully retained shared business assets in violation of common-law conversion principles or fiduciary duties, notwithstanding the terms of the Operating Agreement governing ownership and member withdrawal.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
To prevail on conversion, a plaintiff must show an unauthorized assumption and exercise of the right of ownership over property belonging to the plaintiff. Business assets titled to or owned by an LLC belong to the entity, not to individual members, absent an agreement to the contrary. Fiduciary duty claims by a member require proof of a breach causing damages, evaluated in light of any operating agreement that defines rights and obligations. Contract claims are governed by the plain language of the agreement.

This case concerns a dispute between a former partner and a business associate over the possession of certain business assets following the dissolution of their informal venture. The plaintiff, the former partner, alleges that the defendant wrongfully retained shared equipment, customer records, and funds after the parties ceased operating together. The defendant denies wrongful retention and contends that the assets at issue were either individually owned, lawfully applied to outstanding business obligations, or retained pursuant to the parties’ course of dealing pending final accounting.

### Background

The record shows that the parties operated a small consulting and fabrication business for approximately three years without a comprehensive written partnership agreement. They shared some revenues and expenses, but they also maintained separate accounts, purchased certain tools individually, and used personal property interchangeably for business purposes. When the relationship ended, the plaintiff demanded immediate turnover of all items used in the business and one-half of the remaining funds in the operating account.

The evidence presented at trial included invoices, bank statements, text messages, and testimony from both parties. Several invoices identified the defendant as the sole purchaser of key equipment. Bank records showed that, in the weeks before dissolution, the defendant used business funds to pay rent, vendor balances, and tax liabilities. The plaintiff offered no complete ledger establishing that the retained funds exceeded outstanding obligations or that the disputed equipment had been acquired with joint funds.

The principal issue is whether the defendant wrongfully retained shared business assets in breach of partnership duties or committed conversion by refusing the plaintiff’s demand for immediate possession.

### Applicable Law and Standard

A plaintiff asserting wrongful retention or conversion must prove a superior right to immediate possession of specifically identifiable property. In disputes arising from dissolved partnerships or joint ventures, courts generally require an accounting before one participant may recover an alleged share of undifferentiated business assets, particularly where ownership and liabilities remain disputed. The plaintiff bears the burden of proving joint ownership and wrongful dominion by a preponderance of the evidence.

The plaintiff did not meet that burden. First, the evidence does not establish that all disputed assets were partnership property. The documentary record supports the defendant’s claim that several items were purchased in the defendant’s name with personal funds and later used for business purposes. Mere use in the venture does not, by itself, convert individually owned property into jointly owned property.

Second, as to the retained funds, the record reflects unresolved business debts at the time of dissolution. A partner or joint venturer does not act wrongfully by applying available funds to legitimate business obligations before distribution, absent proof of bad faith or misappropriation. **Opinion**

Plaintiff, an individual homeowner, brought this action against his neighbor alleging defamation arising from statements made during a neighborhood community forum. The trial court entered judgment for defendant, concluding the remarks were either nonactionable opinion or protected by a qualified privilege. Plaintiff appeals. We reverse.

### Background

The record shows that at a monthly community association meeting, defendant stated in front of approximately thirty residents that plaintiff had “stolen money from the neighborhood fund,” “forged signatures on association documents,” and “lied to the board to cover it up.” Plaintiff denied the accusations and presented evidence that no audit, police report, or board finding supported them. Defendant testified that he was “raising concerns” based on rumors he had heard from other residents.

Plaintiff filed suit alleging defamation. The trial court held that the statements were made in a community forum addressing neighborhood governance and therefore were protected expressions of concern. It further concluded that the statements were not provably false because they reflected defendant’s view of plaintiff’s conduct.

### Legal Issue

The issue is whether defendant’s statements at the community forum constitute actionable defamation or are protected as opinion or privileged speech.

### Applicable Law and Standard of Review

To establish defamation, a plaintiff must show a false and defamatory statement of fact concerning the plaintiff, publication to a third party, fault, and resulting harm. Pure opinion is not actionable, but a statement that implies undisclosed defamatory facts, or that can reasonably be understood as asserting objective facts, may support liability. Whether a statement is capable of defamatory meaning is a question of law reviewed de novo.

### Analysis

Defendant’s remarks were not vague expressions of dissatisfaction. Accusations that plaintiff “stole money,” “forged signatures,” and “lied to the board” are specific assertions of criminal and dishonest conduct. Such statements are capable of being proven true or false and would be understood by a reasonable listener as factual allegations, not mere opinion.

Nor does the community-forum setting immunize the statements. While citizens are generally free to discuss neighborhood affairs, that freedom does not extend to knowingly false factual accusations. The record contains no evidence that defendant had a factual basis for the allegations beyond rumor. A speaker cannot avoid defamation liability by couching accusations in the language of concern when the substance of the statement asserts concrete misconduct.

The trial court also erred in treating the statements as privileged. Even assuming a qualified privilege applied to some communications about association matters, that privilege is defeated by publication of unsupported accusations made with reckless disregard for their truth. Defendant’s reliance on rumor, without verification, was insufficient.

### Conclusion

Because defendant’s statements were factual accusations capable of defamatory meaning and were published without adequate basis, the judgment is reversed. The case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion, including determination of damages.

**Background**

The plaintiff and defendant are neighbors in the same subdivision. In the months preceding this action, the parties had disagreed over parking and use of a shared access lane. Shortly thereafter, the defendant posted several messages on the neighborhood forum stating that the plaintiff had “been stealing delivered packages from porches,” was “under police investigation,” and was “known for taking things that do not belong to him.” The posts were visible to forum members, including other residents and the homeowners’ association board.

The plaintiff denied the accusations and presented testimony from a police records custodian establishing that no investigation concerning package theft involving the plaintiff existed. Several neighbors testified that they read the posts and thereafter avoided the plaintiff and discussed the accusations with others. The defendant admitted making the posts but argued they reflected personal belief and neighborhood concern.

**Legal Issue**

The principal issue is whether the defendant’s statements in the community forum constituted actionable defamation rather than protected opinion or rhetorical hyperbole.

**Applicable Law and Standard**

To prevail on a defamation claim under generally applicable state law, a private plaintiff must prove: (1) a false and defamatory statement concerning the plaintiff; (2) publication to a third party; (3) fault amounting at least to negligence; and (4) resulting harm, unless the statement is defamatory per se. Statements accusing a person of criminal conduct are generally defamatory per se. Whether a statement is fact or opinion depends on whether a reasonable reader would understand it as asserting verifiable facts.

**Analysis**

The defendant’s statements were assertions of fact, not mere opinion. Saying that the plaintiff had been “stealing delivered packages” and was “under police investigation” conveys concrete, verifiable events. A reasonable reader would understand those statements as factual claims about criminal conduct. The evidence established falsity: the plaintiff denied the conduct, and official records showed no police investigation. The defendant offered no documentary support, witness testimony, or other reliable basis for the accusations.

Publication is undisputed because the statements were posted to a neighborhood forum accessible to numerous third parties. Fault is likewise established. At minimum, the defendant acted negligently by publishing serious criminal accusations without verifying them. The surrounding dispute between the parties further supports the inference that the statements were made recklessly, if not maliciously.

Finally, the accusations imputed theft, a crime of moral turpitude. Such statements are defamatory per se, and injury to reputation is presumed. In any event, the plaintiff also proved actual reputational harm through testimony that neighbors shunned him and repeated the allegations.

**Conclusion**

The Court finds that the defendant published false factual statements accusing the plaintiff of criminal conduct, that those statements were defamatory, and that the plaintiff suffered compensable harm. Judgment is therefore entered **for the plaintiff**. The plaintiff is entitled to damages in an amount to be determined consistent with this ruling, together with appropriate injunctive relief requiring removal of the defamatory posts.

Whether the statements made by Defendant in the HOA meeting and on the HOA forum are actionable defamatory statements of fact, or are protected opinion, rhetorical hyperbole, or non-actionable privileged communications.

Standard of Review
On a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), the court accepts well-pleaded facts as true and draws reasonable inferences for the plaintiff, but does not accept conclusory allegations. Defamation claims require (1) a false and defamatory statement concerning the plaintiff; (2) publication to a third party; (3) fault amounting at least to negligence; and (4) resulting harm. Pure opinion, inability to prove falsity, or lack of specificity may defeat a claim.

Here, Plaintiff’s complaint alleges that Defendant “accused” Plaintiff of vandalism and theft. The forum posts and meeting comments, as quoted in the complaint, include phrases such as “I think I saw Individual near the broken planter” and “It sure looked like Individual took the package.” These qualify as statements of suspicion and opinion rather than definitive factual assertions. Background
Plaintiff brought a defamation action against Defendant arising from statements made during a publicly noticed meeting of the Bayview Neighborhood Association and in a subsequent post on the association’s online forum. Defendant moved for summary judgment, asserting the statements were substantially true or, alternatively, protected expressions of opinion on a matter of public concern and made without actual malice.

Legal Issue
The primary issues are: (1) whether Defendant’s statements constitute actionable defamation as false assertions of fact rather than opinion; and (2) whether the record demonstrates falsity and the requisite fault under applicable standards.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
To prevail on a defamation claim, a plaintiff must show: (1) a false and defamatory statement of fact; (2) unprivileged publication to a third party; (3) fault amounting at least to negligence for a private figure; and (4) damages. Expressions of opinion that do not reasonably imply undisclosed defamatory facts are not actionable. Statements made in a community forum concerning neighborhood safety and local code compliance are matters of public concern, placing the burden on the plaintiff to prove falsity and, at a minimum, negligence. Summary judgment is appropriate where, viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the nonmovant, no genuine dispute of material fact exists and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.

Analysis
The challenged statements arose from observed conditions: frequent, short-duration occupants at Plaintiff’s residence and multiple listings on a rental website under the street address. Defendant also referenced a city website indicating no active short-term rental permit at that address at the time. In the meeting, Defendant used qualifying language—“appeared to be” and requested clarification from city officials—conveying a tentative assessment based on disclosed facts. On the forum, Defendant linked to the city’s permitting page and the relevant municipal code.

These communications, made in a neighborhood association context, fairly disclosed the underlying facts and invited verification. As such, they are nonactionable opinion or, at a minimum, not reasonably understood as asserting undisclosed defamatory facts. Even if treated as factual, Plaintiff has not produced competent evidence of falsity at the time of publication. Plaintiff’s later-acquired permit does not negate the absence of a permit when Defendant spoke. Nor has Plaintiff shown fault; Defendant consulted public sources and reported personal observations, which is reasonable care under the circumstances. There is also no evidence of actual malice.

Finally, Plaintiff’s damages showing—generalized embarrassment and speculative lost tenants—lacks admissible evidence tying any specific pecuniary loss to Defendant’s statements.

Because Plaintiff has not established a triable issue on falsity, actionable fact versus opinion, or fault, Defendant’s motion for summary judgment is GRANTED. Judgment shall enter for Defendant on all claims. Each party shall bear its own costs.

Background

This case concerns a dispute between Plaintiff, a freelance service provider (hereafter "Provider"), and Defendant, a client (hereafter "Client"), over payment for completed services. Provider alleges Client breached a written agreement by failing to pay the final invoice for services rendered. Client contends either that the work was incomplete or defective, or that a setoff for alleged damages excuses payment. Provider seeks the unpaid balance plus pre-judgment interest and costs.

Legal Issue

Whether Provider is entitled to recover the unpaid contract balance for completed services under the parties' written agreement, notwithstanding Client's asserted defenses of defective performance and setoff.

Applicable Law / Standard of Review

Under general contract principles, a plaintiff asserting breach must prove formation of a contract, performance by the plaintiff, defendant's breach, and resulting damages. Where a service contract is expressed in writing, the court enforces its clear terms. Defenses of nonpayment or setoff require proof that the alleged defects were material and that the defendant provided timely notice and an opportunity to cure, if required by the contract. Findings of fact are reviewed for clear error and legal conclusions de novo.

Analysis

The written agreement, signed by both parties, specified a defined scope of services, fixed milestones, and payment schedule culminating in a final invoice upon completion of the agreed deliverables. The record shows Provider submitted the final deliverables and issued the final invoice per the contract schedule. Client acknowledged receipt of the deliverables in contemporaneous communications and accepted them for use without timely objection.

Client's principal defense is that the work was defective and therefore entitlement to payment is excused. The evidence does not support a material-defect claim. Client produced no expert or persuasive objective proof that the deliverables failed to conform to the contract specifications. Client's internal emails reflect dissatisfaction with aesthetic choices and a desire for further revisions, but the contract expressly limited revision obligations and required that additional work be compensated. Because Client accepted the deliverables and did not follow the contract's notice-and-cure procedures, the defense of defective performance is unavailing.

Client also asserts a setoff for alleged consequential losses. Contract law typically limits setoff to amounts expressly agreed or to damages properly proven. Client failed to quantify the alleged losses or link them causally to Provider's performance. Nor does the record show a contractual right to unilateral setoff.

Accordingly, Provider has established formation, performance, Client's breach by nonpayment, and damages equal to the unpaid invoice amount. Pre-judgment interest is allowable under the contract's forum law clause and general principles that compensate for the time value of money.

Conclusion

Judgment is entered for Plaintiff. Provider is awarded the unpaid contract balance as set forth in the final invoice, together with pre-judgment interest and costs. The Clerk is directed to enter judgment accordingly.

Legal Issue

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
A plaintiff alleging breach of contract must prove: (1) existence of a valid contract; (2) plaintiff’s performance or substantial performance; (3) defendant’s breach; and (4) resulting damages. Where a contract provides for procedures to dispute invoices or reject work, failure to comply may constitute waiver of those objections. An account stated arises when a debtor retains an invoice without timely objection, creating a new promise to pay the stated balance. The party asserting nonconforming performance bears the burden to show material breach excusing payment.

Analysis
The MSA is undisputed and valid. It requires payment within 30 days and provides that any dispute regarding charges or deliverables must be raised in writing within 10 business days of invoice or delivery, identifying the specific basis. Damages are the unpaid principal of $18,750. Prejudgment interest is appropriate under the MSA at 1% per month from the invoice due dates.

Judgment is entered for plaintiff ServicePro LLC in the amount of $18,750, plus contractual prejudgment interest and costs. North Ridge Outfitters, Inc. breached the MSA by failing to pay for accepted services and failed to preserve any objections to the invoices or deliverables.

Defendant’s project manager acknowledged receipt and requested minor revisions, which Plaintiff implemented within five days. Before the scheduled acceptance meeting, Defendant emailed a cancellation citing “strategic reprioritization,” refused to issue payment for Milestone One, and demanded turnover of all work product without compensation. Plaintiff sued for breach of contract and, alternatively, quantum meruit. Following a bench trial on stipulated exhibits and testimony, the matter is submitted for decision.

Legal Issue
Whether Defendant wrongfully terminated the project without paying for completed work, breaching the contract’s milestone and termination provisions, and, failing that, whether Plaintiff is entitled to recovery in quantum meruit.

To establish breach of contract, a plaintiff must show a valid contract, performance or substantial performance, the defendant’s breach, and resulting damages. Contract terms are enforced according to their plain meaning. A termination-for-convenience clause generally requires compliance with stated notice provisions and payment for work performed to date. Quantum meruit permits recovery of the reasonable value of services conferred and accepted to prevent unjust enrichment where no enforceable contract governs the compensation at issue.

The parties’ written agreement is undisputed. The core dispute is whether Plaintiff completed Milestone One and whether Defendant’s cancellation relieved it of payment. The termination clause allowed cancellation upon seven days’ written notice “with payment for services rendered through the effective date.” Defendant’s same-day cancellation email did not provide seven days’ notice and expressly refused payment. The contract did not condition payment on formal sign-off where deliverables met specified criteria and acceptance was not unreasonably withheld. Because the contract governs, the Court need not reach quantum meruit except in the alternative. Were it necessary, the evidence would support recovery of the reasonable value of the services, as Defendant received and retains the benefit of the work product.

Judgment is entered for Plaintiff on the breach of contract claim in the amount of $12,000, plus prejudgment interest as allowed by law and costs. Defendant’s counterarguments are denied. The Clerk shall enter judgment accordingly.

The SOW incorporated Defendant’s standard Master Services Agreement (MSA), which included: (1) a termination-for-convenience clause allowing either party to terminate on seven days’ written notice, with payment due for “Services satisfactorily performed and accepted as of the effective date of termination”; (2) an acceptance procedure requiring written acceptance or a written list of deficiencies within five business days after delivery; and (3) a change-order provision for material scope changes.

Plaintiff delivered a beta on February 16, 2025, one day late. On February 19, Defendant sent a written notice identifying deficiencies including inaccurate SKU sync, intermittent timeouts, and failure to meet specified reporting formats. On February 26, after additional testing, Defendant issued a termination-for-convenience notice effective March 4, 2025. Plaintiff submitted an invoice for the first milestone and additional hours for remediation. Defendant declined payment, asserting the beta was neither timely nor accepted. Plaintiff sued for breach of contract and, in the alternative, unjust enrichment.

Legal Issue
Whether Defendant wrongfully terminated the project and failed to pay for completed work that was allegedly accepted or otherwise compensable.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
Contract interpretation is a question of law. The court enforces unambiguous provisions according to their plain meaning. A party invoking termination-for-convenience must comply with notice requirements and pay amounts due under the contract. Milestone payments contingent on acceptance are not owed absent acceptance or waiver. Unjust enrichment is unavailable where an enforceable contract governs the subject matter.

The MSA unambiguously conditions milestone payments on “Services satisfactorily performed and accepted.” The SOW ties the first milestone to delivery of a functional beta by a date certain. Plaintiff does not dispute the listed defects but contends they were curable and largely resolved before termination. No writing in the record reflects acceptance or waiver by Defendant.

Defendant complied with the termination-for-convenience provision by providing seven days’ written notice effective March 4. Under the MSA, upon such termination, payment is due only for services “satisfactorily performed and accepted” as of the effective date. Because the beta was neither accepted nor shown to conform to specifications, the contractual trigger for the first milestone did not occur. The extra remediation hours also fall within the governed subject matter and likewise require acceptance or an approved change order, which is absent here.

Plaintiff’s unjust enrichment claim fails because an enforceable contract defines the parties’ rights and remedies, including the allocation of risk for non-accepted work.

Defendant lawfully terminated under the contract and did not breach by withholding milestone payment for an unaccepted, nonconforming beta. Judgment is entered for Defendant on all claims. Each party shall bear its own costs.

Plaintiff, a co-owner of a residential parcel and attached driveway, brought suit after Defendant changed the locks on a shared gate, blocked access to the driveway with parked vehicles, and refused Plaintiff repeated requests for entry. Plaintiff sought declaratory and injunctive relief, as well as damages for loss of use. Defendant argued that, as a co-owner, he had equal rights to control access and that his actions were justified by disputes over maintenance and expenses.

### Background

The parties inherited the property from a family member and hold title as tenants in common. The record shows that Plaintiff regularly used the driveway and storage area on the property for personal and business purposes. After a disagreement over repair costs, Defendant installed a new lock on the gate and did not provide Plaintiff a key. Defendant also placed vehicles and equipment in the driveway, preventing Plaintiff from entering with a trailer. Plaintiff testified that he was denied access for several months despite multiple written demands. Defendant did not dispute the exclusion but contended that Plaintiff had failed to contribute to upkeep and therefore should not be permitted to use the property until he paid.

### Legal Issue

The central issue is whether a co-owner may unilaterally exclude another co-owner from the common property absent a court order, agreement, or legally recognized necessity.

### Applicable Law and Standard of Review

Under basic principles of co-tenancy, each tenant in common has an equal right to possess and use the whole property, subject to the equal rights of the other co-owners. A co-owner may not oust another co-owner from possession without lawful justification. Where exclusion is shown, the excluded co-owner may seek injunctive relief and damages for wrongful deprivation of use. The court reviews the facts for clear preponderance and applies settled property law to determine whether Defendant’s conduct amounted to an ouster.

### Analysis

The evidence establishes that Plaintiff had a lawful possessory interest in the property and that Defendant intentionally interfered with that interest. Changing the lock without providing access, combined with physical obstruction of the driveway, went beyond ordinary management of shared property. Defendant’s asserted justification—that Plaintiff had not paid maintenance expenses—does not authorize self-help exclusion. A co-owner’s remedy for contribution disputes lies in accounting, partition, or judicial enforcement, not unilateral denial of access.

The record also supports a finding of ouster. Plaintiff made repeated demands for access, and Defendant refused. The exclusion was not temporary or incidental; it persisted for months and prevented Plaintiff from using the property in the manner consistent with his ownership rights. Defendant therefore breached Plaintiff’s equal right of possession.

### Conclusion

The court finds for Plaintiff. Defendant unlawfully excluded Plaintiff from the shared property and is enjoined from interfering with Plaintiff’s reasonable access and use. Plaintiff is entitled to damages for the period of wrongful exclusion, to be determined on the submitted record or at further hearing if necessary.

The record shows that the property contains a cabin, a storage shed, and an access road crossing open land. For several months, the parties had an informal arrangement under which each used the property independently. After a series of vandalism incidents, the defendant replaced the gate lock and installed a notice requesting that all visitors contact him before entering. The plaintiff later arrived without prior notice, found the gate locked, and was told by the defendant that he could enter only after coordinating access to avoid further damage. The plaintiff filed suit, alleging exclusion from shared property and seeking damages and injunctive relief.

The central issue is whether the defendant’s conduct amounted to an unlawful ouster or exclusion of a co-owner from lawful use of jointly owned property.

As a general rule, each co-owner has the right to possess and use the entire property, subject to the equal rights of the other co-owner. Smith, Plaintiff,
v.
Lopez, Defendant.

Opinion and Order

Background
Plaintiff, the owner of 214 Maple Lane, brought an action for encroachment and ejectment alleging that Defendant, the adjacent landowner at 216 Maple Lane, constructed a six-foot privacy fence that extends 1.8 feet over the common boundary and onto Plaintiff’s parcel. Plaintiff seeks declaratory relief establishing the boundary line, removal of the encroaching portion of the fence, and nominal damages. Defendant denies encroachment, contends the fence follows an historical line marked by an old hedgerow, and alternatively asserts acquiescence or adverse possession based on long-standing use.

After a bench trial, the Court received testimony from both parties, a licensed surveyor retained by Plaintiff, and a fencing contractor retained by Defendant. The Court also admitted into evidence the recorded deeds for both parcels, a 2012 subdivision plat, and a 2023 boundary survey prepared for Plaintiff.

Legal Issue
The principal issues are: (1) whether the fence encroaches on Plaintiff’s property; and, if so, (2) whether Defendant has established a legal basis—by acquiescence or adverse possession—to maintain the fence where it stands.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
Encroachment is established where a structure extends beyond the boundary of the owner’s land onto another’s property. A plaintiff must prove encroachment by a preponderance of the evidence. Adverse possession requires open, notorious, continuous, exclusive, and hostile possession under claim of right for the statutory period. Acquiescence to a boundary generally requires mutual recognition of a line as the boundary for the statutory period. Equitable relief for a continuing encroachment may include mandatory removal where legal remedies are inadequate.

Analysis
The deeds and the 2012 recorded plat describe the common boundary as a straight line running due north-south from a monumented iron pin at the sidewalk to a rear corner marked on the plat. Plaintiff’s surveyor credibly testified that he recovered the front iron pin, reestablished the rear corner using the plat’s bearings and distances, and located the fence line extending 1.8 feet east of the true boundary onto Plaintiff’s parcel along a run of approximately 48 feet. His methodology conformed to accepted surveying practices, and his field notes and measurements were consistent with the recorded plat.

Defendant’s contractor did not perform a boundary survey and relied on a visible hedgerow and an older chain-link fence remnant as guides. That testimony does not overcome the recorded instruments and professional survey. The Court finds that Plaintiff has proven encroachment by a preponderance of the evidence.

Defendant’s defenses fail. The record shows the current fence was installed in 2021, well short of any statutory period for adverse possession. The prior hedgerow and deteriorated fence remnants, to the extent they wandered over the line, were neither shown to be installed or maintained under a claim of right nor to satisfy exclusivity and continuity. With respect to acquiescence, there is no evidence of a mutual agreement or long-term mutual recognition of the hedgerow as the legal boundary; Plaintiff purchased in 2019 and promptly objected upon commissioning the 2023 survey.

A continuing encroachment onto land constitutes an ongoing injury not adequately remedied by damages. Given the modest cost to adjust the fence and the clear boundary evidence, equitable removal is appropriate.

Conclusion
Judgment is entered for Plaintiff. The Court declares the true boundary as reflected in the 2012 subdivision plat and Plaintiff’s 2023 survey. Defendant shall, within 45 days, remove or relocate the encroaching portion of the fence to the true boundary line. Plaintiff is awarded nominal damages of $1 and costs. Each party shall otherwise bear its own fees. SO ORDERED.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT OF HAWTHORNE COUNTY

Miller v. Ortega

Background
Plaintiff Sarah Miller owns a residential parcel at 214 Grove Street. Defendant Carlos Ortega owns the adjacent parcel at 216 Grove Street. In 2022, Ortega replaced an aging wooden fence separating the properties with a new vinyl fence. Miller alleges the new fence encroaches 1.2 feet onto her property along a 60-foot stretch. Ortega asserts he placed the fence along the historic boundary line based on a boundary line agreement reached by the parties’ predecessors in interest in 2005 and visible monuments long recognized by both lots’ owners. Miller seeks an order compelling removal of the alleged encroachment and damages for trespass.

Legal Issue
The principal issues are: (1) whether the fence lies on Miller’s property; and, if so, (2) whether Ortega may nevertheless rely on a prior boundary line agreement or acquiescence to establish the boundary where the fence now stands.

Applicable Law/Standard of Review
In a boundary dispute, the plaintiff bears the burden to prove encroachment by a preponderance of the evidence. Recorded deeds control unless the parties, or their predecessors, have established a boundary by agreement or long-standing acquiescence, supported by definite, visible monuments and mutual recognition. A boundary by acquiescence may be found where adjoining owners mutually treat a line as the boundary for a substantial period, typically exceeding the statute of limitations period for ejectment. Equitable defenses such as laches may also apply where a landowner unreasonably delays asserting known boundary claims to the prejudice of the adjoining owner.

Analysis
Miller presented a 2023 survey prepared by Douglas & Hart Surveyors locating the deeded boundary based on bearings and distances in the 1989 subdivision plat. The survey places the fence 1.2 feet inside Miller’s parcel. Ortega countered with: (a) a 2005 written boundary line agreement between the then-owners, Rodriguez and Bennett, identifying the “centerline of existing hedge and fence” as the common boundary, with an attached sketch; (b) testimony from Ortega and a neighbor that, from 2005 until the 2022 replacement, the parties maintained and treated the old fence line as the boundary; and (c) photographs and a contractor’s testimony that the 2022 fence was installed along the same line, using existing post footings and string lines tied to the prior fence and hedge.

Although Miller’s survey is competent evidence of the deed line, the 2005 agreement, which is signed, notarized, and recorded, establishes a boundary by agreement tied to a visible monument—the prior fence/hedge line. The evidence shows continuous mutual recognition and maintenance of that line for more than fifteen years. Miller acquired her property in 2018 subject to matters of record and apparent conditions observable on inspection, which included the existing fence at the agreed line. Her predecessor did not object, and Miller likewise voiced no objection until after Ortega replaced deteriorated materials in kind. On this record, the boundary established by agreement and acquiescence controls over the deed description as between these adjacent owners.

Because the 2022 fence follows the agreed boundary, there is no encroachment, and the trespass claim fails. Alternatively, Miller’s delay and Ortega’s good-faith reliance would bar equitable relief.

Conclusion
Judgment is entered for Defendant Carlos Ortega. The complaint is dismissed with prejudice. Each party shall bear its own costs.
