In disputes over repair charges, the Court applies ordinary principles of contract and quasi-contract. A repair shop generally may not impose charges for wholly unauthorized work. The Court evaluates the evidence under a preponderance standard.

The evidence supports Defendant’s position. Plaintiff entrusted the vehicle to Defendant for diagnosis of a breakdown involving overheating and stalling. The repairs performed were not unrelated upgrades or elective services; they directly addressed the diagnosed cause of the failure and the immediately resulting damage. Moreover, the circumstances justified prompt action. The credible testimony established that delaying repair would likely have caused additional engine damage and substantially increased cost. Under these facts, Defendant acted within the reasonable scope of the service relationship to preserve the vehicle from further harm. Buyer, Plaintiff,
v.
Seller, Defendant.

OPINION AND ORDER

Background
Plaintiff contracted to purchase 500 custom-fabricated steel panels from Defendant for use in a commercial renovation project. The contract incorporated standard UCC terms and required delivery by March 1. Defendant delivered the panels on February 25. Upon receipt, Plaintiff’s site superintendent noted visible surface pitting and minor dimensional variances on a portion of the panels and documented these conditions in an internal report. Plaintiff nonetheless directed installation to proceed due to schedule constraints. Over the next three weeks, Plaintiff installed approximately 420 panels, invoiced its own client for progress billing, and made partial payment to Defendant for 80% of the contract price. One month after delivery, Plaintiff sent Defendant a written notice purporting to reject the entire shipment and demanded a refund, asserting nonconformity. Defendant refused, asserting that Plaintiff accepted the goods under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC).

Legal Issue
Whether Plaintiff accepted the goods within the meaning of the UCC despite awareness of defects, thereby precluding rejection and limiting Plaintiff’s remedy to damages for any nonconformity.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
Under UCC § 2-606, a buyer accepts goods when, after a reasonable opportunity to inspect, the buyer signifies that the goods are conforming or that the buyer will retain them despite nonconformity; fails to make an effective rejection under § 2-602; or acts inconsistently with the seller’s ownership. Acceptance of part of a commercial unit is acceptance of the whole unit. Under § 2-602, rejection must be within a reasonable time after delivery or tender and requires seasonable notice. After acceptance, the buyer may revoke only under § 2-608 upon showing a substantial impairment not discovered due to difficulty of discovery or seller’s assurances, and must do so within a reasonable time after discovery. The buyer bears the burden to show effective rejection or revocation.

Analysis
Plaintiff had a reasonable opportunity to inspect at delivery; its superintendent observed and recorded the defects. Despite that knowledge, Plaintiff proceeded to install the majority of the panels, billed its customer, and remitted substantial payment to Defendant. These actions are inconsistent with Defendant’s ownership and constitute acceptance under § 2-606(1)(c). Further, Plaintiff did not seasonably reject. The written notice issued approximately thirty days after delivery, after extensive installation and use, falls outside a reasonable time given the apparent nature of the defects and Plaintiff’s immediate awareness.

Nor has Plaintiff established grounds for revocation under § 2-608. The defects were discovered at delivery; there is no evidence of assurances by Defendant causing delayed discovery, and Plaintiff’s continued installation after discovery undermines any claim of substantial impairment justifying revocation. Any remedy therefore lies in damages for any proven nonconformity, not rejection of the goods or refund of the contract price.

Conclusion
Plaintiff accepted the goods despite known defects and failed to effect a timely rejection or valid revocation. Defendant is entitled to judgment on Plaintiff’s claim for rejection and refund. The complaint is dismissed with prejudice as to rejection-based relief. This ruling is without prejudice to Plaintiff’s right, if any, to pursue damages for nonconformity consistent with the UCC and the parties’ contract.

So ordered.

The customer alleges that the service provider advertised specific features and performance levels that were not delivered after payment was made. The service provider denies any wrongdoing and contends that its promotional materials were merely general statements of quality and not enforceable promises.

### Background

The customer purchased a premium home maintenance plan from the service provider after reviewing written marketing materials and speaking with a sales representative. According to the customer, the provider represented that the plan included same-day emergency response, unlimited service calls, and coverage for all labor costs. After the customer experienced a plumbing failure, however, the provider responded two days later, limited the number of visits, and charged additional labor fees. The customer filed suit alleging misrepresentation and deceptive trade practices.

The service provider argues that the customer received the contract terms and that any promotional statements were nonbinding puffery. It further contends that the written agreement contained a general disclaimer stating that services were subject to availability and that certain exclusions applied.

### Legal Issue

The central issue is whether the service provider materially misrepresented the nature and scope of the services before the customer purchased the plan, such that the customer was induced to contract on false premises.

### Applicable Law and Standard of Review

A claim for misrepresentation generally requires proof that: (1) the defendant made a false statement of material fact; (2) the defendant knew or should have known the statement was false; (3) the statement was intended to induce reliance; (4) the plaintiff reasonably relied on it; and (5) damages resulted. Courts distinguish actionable factual representations from vague sales talk or puffery. Contract disclaimers may limit liability, but they do not automatically defeat a claim where specific pre-sale representations contradict the written terms or where the disclaimer is not sufficiently clear and conspicuous.

### Analysis

The record supports the customer’s claim. The provider’s marketing materials did not merely praise the quality of its services; they made specific, measurable promises regarding response time, number of visits, and labor coverage. Those statements concern concrete facts, not opinion. The customer relied on them in deciding to purchase the plan, and that reliance was reasonable given the specificity of the representations.

The provider’s disclaimer does not alter the result. Although the agreement referenced availability and exclusions, it did not clearly negate the earlier promises of same-day response and unlimited calls. A general disclaimer cannot be used to erase precise pre-contract assurances that formed the basis of the bargain. The evidence also shows that the provider’s actual performance fell materially short of what was promised.

### Conclusion

The Court finds that the service provider misrepresented the services before purchase and that the customer reasonably relied on those misrepresentations. Judgment is entered for the plaintiff, the customer. Appropriate relief shall be determined consistent with this opinion.

Within weeks, Plaintiff experienced repeated service interruptions and discovered that the package did not include live monitoring by technicians, but instead relied on automated alerts reviewed only during business hours. The “automatic threat removal” feature required separate customer approval and additional fees, and several household devices were excluded from coverage under terms disclosed only after purchase in a customer portal. Plaintiff sought a refund. Defendant denied the request, citing a limitation-of-liability clause and a provision stating that detailed service terms were incorporated by reference.

Plaintiff filed suit alleging misrepresentation and violation of state consumer protection law. After a bench trial, the Court now enters judgment.

**Legal Issues**

The principal issue is whether Defendant materially misrepresented the nature and scope of its services before purchase, such that Plaintiff is entitled to relief for deceptive trade practices and common-law misrepresentation.

**Applicable Law and Standard of Review**

A plaintiff alleging actionable misrepresentation must generally show a false statement of material fact, made in connection with a transaction, on which the plaintiff reasonably relied, causing damages. Consumer protection statutes likewise prohibit deceptive or misleading acts likely to mislead a reasonable consumer. In evaluating such claims, the Court considers the net impression created by pre-sale statements, not isolated disclaimers revealed only after the transaction. Contractual limitations do not bar claims based on fraud or deception in the inducement.

**Analysis**

The evidence establishes that Defendant’s pre-purchase representations were materially inaccurate. The phrase “24/7 live technician monitoring” conveyed continuous human oversight. Defendant’s own internal service documents, however, showed that no such around-the-clock technician review existed. Likewise, “automatic threat removal” suggested included remediation without further action or charge, yet the service required additional authorization and fees. Finally, “full-device coverage for all household electronics” was contradicted by exclusions for gaming consoles, smart appliances, and older mobile devices.

These were not minor ambiguities. They concerned the core value of the service package and would plainly matter to a reasonable consumer deciding whether to purchase. Plaintiff credibly testified that these features were the reason for selecting Defendant’s premium plan over lower-cost alternatives. That reliance was reasonable because the contradictory limitations were not clearly disclosed before purchase. A buried hyperlink or post-sale portal disclosure cannot cure affirmative, prominent representations made during marketing.

Defendant’s reliance on contractual disclaimers is unavailing. A seller may define service terms, but it may not induce a sale through statements that materially overstate what is being sold. The Court therefore finds that Defendant’s conduct was deceptive and constituted actionable misrepresentation.

**Conclusion**

Judgment is entered in favor of Plaintiff Customer. Plaintiff is entitled to rescission of the service contract, a refund of amounts paid, and such statutory costs and other relief as may be determined upon further submission. Defendant’s pre-purchase statements materially misrepresented the services offered, and Plaintiff purchased the package in reasonable reliance on those statements.

Jane Miller, Plaintiff,
v.
TechGuard Home Services, LLC, Defendant.

Opinion

Background
Plaintiff Jane Miller purchased a one-year home security monitoring plan from Defendant TechGuard Home Services, LLC after reviewing the company’s website and speaking with a sales representative by phone. Miller alleges that Defendant misrepresented the scope of monitoring and response times, claiming “24/7 professional monitoring” and “instant police dispatch.” After a burglary at Miller’s residence, the system transmitted an alert, a TechGuard operator called Miller within two minutes, and law enforcement was notified nine minutes later. Miller contends the response fell short of what was promised and sues for fraudulent misrepresentation and violation of the state consumer protection statute. Defendant denies misrepresentation and points to written terms delivered at purchase and in a confirmation email stating that response times may vary, dispatch requires verification consistent with local protocols, and no outcome is guaranteed.

Legal Issues
The issues are: (1) whether Plaintiff has shown actionable misrepresentation—false representation of material fact, reasonable reliance, and resulting damages; and (2) whether the marketing statements constitute deceptive acts under the consumer protection statute.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
To prevail on fraudulent misrepresentation, a plaintiff must establish by a preponderance of the evidence a false statement of material fact, knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard, intent to induce reliance, justifiable reliance, and damages caused thereby. Puffery or generalized promotional language is not actionable. For statutory deception, the standard is whether the act is likely to mislead a reasonable consumer, considering the advertisement as a whole, including qualifying disclosures. Contractual terms and clear disclaimers are relevant to the reasonableness of reliance and the likelihood of deception.

Analysis
Plaintiff relies primarily on two phrases: “24/7 professional monitoring” and “instant police dispatch.” The record shows TechGuard operates a staffed monitoring center continuously, which matches the literal representation. The phrase “instant police dispatch,” while in bold on a webpage banner, is immediately followed by an asterisk and a footnote: “Dispatch initiated upon alarm verification; response times vary by jurisdiction and conditions.” The purchase confirmation email and service agreement reiterate that verification may be required by law or local policy, and no specific response time is guaranteed.

In context, “instant police dispatch” is non-specific promotional language tempered by conspicuous qualifying disclosures. Courts routinely deem such general superiority claims and time-related slogans to be non-actionable puffery when paired with clear limitations. Plaintiff has not shown that Defendant promised a definite response time or unconditional automatic dispatch. Nor is there evidence Defendant knew any representation was false at the time made. The undisputed timeline—a two-minute operator call and a nine-minute initiation of police notification—aligns with the disclosed verification process and varying response conditions. Any reliance on an absolute, unconditional interpretation would be unreasonable in light of the simultaneously presented disclaimers and written terms.

As to the consumer protection claim, considering the advertisement as a whole, including the asterisked footnote and the agreement’s prominent disclosures sent immediately upon purchase, Plaintiff has not shown a likely tendency to mislead a reasonable consumer about the nature of monitoring or dispatch contingencies.

Conclusion
Plaintiff has failed to establish actionable misrepresentation or a deceptive act. Judgment is entered for Defendant TechGuard Home Services, LLC on all claims. Each party shall bear its own costs.

On a motion for judgment on the pleadings, the court accepts well-pleaded facts as true and construes them in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party, but the moving party prevails if the complaint fails to state a plausible claim. Under controlling principles, an integration clause and explicit, detailed contract terms generally preclude reliance on prior inconsistent oral statements. Where the written contract unambiguously discloses limitations, a plaintiff’s allegation that a vague oral promise induced the purchase is insufficient without pleading specific factual circumstances showing that the written terms were themselves false, that the supplier engaged in affirmative concealment, or that the integration clause was procured by fraud. Plaintiff’s complaint alleges neither that the written terms were false nor that Defendant concealed exclusions; it rests on an ambiguous adjective “comprehensive” and on supposed statements by an unnamed representative. Nguyen contends Ellis agreed to “pay me back when you’re better,” but no written agreement was executed, and Ellis later declined to reimburse certain charges, disputing their necessity and amount. Ellis admits illness and acknowledges that Nguyen advanced funds for some items but denies any enforceable promise to repay beyond a modest cash repayment already made, and further characterizes much of the expense as voluntary or excessive.

Legal Issue
Whether Nguyen is entitled to reimbursement based on an enforceable contract or, alternatively, under the equitable doctrine of unjust enrichment/necessaries for emergency expenses advanced on Ellis’s behalf.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
To prevail on a breach of contract claim, a plaintiff must establish offer, acceptance, consideration, and sufficiently definite terms. Oral agreements may be enforceable, but their material terms must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence. Under unjust enrichment, a plaintiff must show (1) the defendant received a benefit, (2) at the plaintiff’s expense, and (3) under circumstances that make it unjust for the defendant to retain the benefit without payment. Recovery is limited to the reasonable value of necessary goods or services actually conferred. Voluntary payments made officiously, or expenses that are not reasonably necessary, are not recoverable.

Analysis
Nguyen’s contract claim fails. The alleged statement—“pay me back when you’re better”—is too indefinite to establish a binding promise as to the scope or amount of repayment. The record contains no contemporaneous writing, itemized assent, or mutual understanding allocating which expenses would be reimbursed. The parties’ subsequent text messages reflect appreciation by Ellis but no agreement on specific sums or categories. Absent definite terms, the court cannot imply an obligation to repay every expense Nguyen unilaterally chose to incur.

Turning to unjust enrichment, Nguyen did confer some benefit: Ellis used transportation to reach medical care and received prescribed medication. However, Nguyen bears the burden to prove the reasonable value of necessary services. The evidence shows bundled ride-share charges, premium hotel extension fees, restaurant deliveries, and over-the-counter items not prescribed. Nguyen provided no receipts segregating medically necessary costs from convenience expenditures, nor expert or provider testimony on necessity. Moreover, Ellis credibly testified that he offered to contact his insurer and a family member for assistance and objected to the upgraded hotel room and multiple delivery orders. On this record, Nguyen has not established, by a preponderance of the evidence, either an enforceable agreement or that Ellis was unjustly enriched beyond the amount already repaid. The court will not impose liability for voluntary, inadequately substantiated, or nonessential expenditures.

Judgment is entered for Defendant Jordan Ellis. Plaintiff Alex Nguyen’s claims for breach of contract and unjust enrichment are denied. Each party shall bear his own costs.

Plaintiff contends that Defendant expressed gratitude and said, “I’ll make this right,” but no specific repayment terms were discussed. Defendant recovered and later offered to reimburse the cost of ride-share transport only, which Plaintiff declined. Plaintiff then filed this action seeking full reimbursement under theories of implied-in-fact contract, implied-in-law (quasi-contract) unjust enrichment, and necessity.

Legal Issue
Whether Defendant is legally obligated to reimburse Plaintiff for emergency-related expenses paid voluntarily and without an express agreement, under theories of implied contract or unjust enrichment.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
To establish an implied-in-fact contract, a plaintiff must show mutual assent inferred from conduct and sufficiently definite terms. An unjust enrichment claim in quasi-contract requires proof that (1) the plaintiff conferred a benefit on the defendant, (2) the defendant appreciated and accepted the benefit, and (3) it would be inequitable to retain the benefit without payment. However, benefits conferred officiously or as “good Samaritan” acts without a reasonable expectation of compensation are generally not recoverable. Medical necessity may justify restitution where the recipient is unable to consent and the services are necessary to prevent serious harm, and where the provider reasonably expects compensation.

Analysis
Plaintiff’s implied-in-fact contract claim fails. The record shows no discussion of repayment terms, no agreement on amount, timing, or scope, and no request by Defendant that Plaintiff pay the clinic or purchase supplies. Defendant’s statement, “I’ll make this right,” is insufficiently definite to constitute mutual assent to a binding obligation for all expenses. Absent objective manifestations of agreement, the law does not infer contractual liability.

The unjust enrichment theory also fails. Plaintiff conferred a benefit by facilitating transport and treatment, and Defendant accepted the treatment. Yet equity does not mandate reimbursement where the benefit was conferred voluntarily, without solicitation, and under circumstances suggesting a gratuitous rescue among friends. The ankle injury, while painful, did not render Defendant incapable of consenting; Defendant could have chosen the level of care or payment arrangements. Plaintiff did not demonstrate a contemporaneous expectation of compensation communicated to Defendant. The offer to cover ride-share costs, which Plaintiff refused, further indicates the absence of a shared understanding as to broader reimbursement and weighs against inequity in Defendant’s partial stance.

Finally, the medical necessity exception to the volunteer rule is inapplicable. Defendant was conscious and able to make decisions. Restitution for emergency services is typically reserved for providers or circumstances where consent is impossible and services are necessary to prevent serious harm. Plaintiff is not a medical provider, and the facts do not show imminent life-threatening peril requiring unilateral financial commitment.

Because Plaintiff has not established an implied-in-fact contract, and restitution is unwarranted under unjust enrichment principles, judgment is entered for Defendant. Each party shall bear their own costs.

The guaranty provided that Trent “absolutely and unconditionally” guaranteed payment of the borrower’s obligations in the event of default.

In 2023, Harbor defaulted after failing to make required payments. The bank demanded payment from both Harbor and Trent. A guaranty is interpreted according to ordinary contract principles. Where the language is clear, courts enforce it as written. A guarantor who pays the debt of a principal obligor is generally entitled to reimbursement and equitable subrogation unless the guaranty was discharged by a material, unauthorized alteration of the underlying obligation. Minor extensions, payment accommodations, or modifications expressly permitted by the guaranty do not discharge the guarantor.

The guaranty here is broad and explicit. It states that Trent’s obligations would not be affected by “renewal, extension, modification, compromise, or release” granted to the borrower, and that Trent waived notice of such actions. The total indebtedness remained within the original credit limit, the interest formula did not change, and no new category of liability was added. For the District

Loan Guarantor (Plaintiff)
v.
Primary Borrower (Defendant)

OPINION AND ORDER

Background
This action arises from a business loan made by Lender to Defendant, who is the primary borrower, with Plaintiff serving as a guarantor under a written guaranty agreement. Defendant defaulted on the loan by failing to make scheduled payments and by breaching a covenant to maintain certain collateral. Lender sought payment from Plaintiff under the guaranty; Plaintiff sued Defendant seeking declaratory and monetary relief, asserting that (1) Defendant’s default and subsequent actions discharged Plaintiff’s obligations as guarantor, and (2) Defendant must indemnify Plaintiff for amounts paid to Lender. The parties filed cross-motions for summary judgment. For the reasons below, the Court grants summary judgment for Plaintiff.

Legal Issues
1. Whether Plaintiff remains liable under the guaranty following Defendant’s default and subsequent conduct.
2. Whether Defendant must indemnify Plaintiff for amounts Plaintiff paid to Lender under the guaranty.

Applicable Law / Standard of Review
Interpretation of written guaranty and indemnity agreements is governed by contract law. Summary judgment is appropriate where there is no genuine dispute of material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. A guarantor’s obligations may be discharged by material alteration of the underlying loan terms, failure of the lender to comply with notice or collection provisions that prejudice the guarantor, or by contractual conditions precedent. Indemnity obligations are enforced according to their plain terms.

Analysis
The guaranty here is an unconditional, continuing guaranty obligating Plaintiff to pay "all amounts due under the Loan Agreement," subject to the lender’s compliance with notice requirements and reasonable collection efforts. The undisputed record shows: (1) after Defendant’s default, Defendant unilaterally executed an amendment to the Loan Agreement that materially altered the payment schedule and subordinated Plaintiff’s interest without Plaintiff’s consent; (2) Lender accepted the amendment without obtaining Plaintiff’s written consent and failed to provide required notice of default and acceleration consistent with the guaranty; and (3) Plaintiff paid the outstanding balance to avoid foreclosure after reasonable but unsuccessful attempts to obtain cure from Defendant.

Under established contract principles, a material, unconsented alteration to the principal obligation discharges a guarantor to the extent the alteration prejudices the guarantor. The amendment here increased Plaintiff’s exposure by extending payment terms and altering collateral priorities; acceptance without Plaintiff’s consent therefore discharged Plaintiff from future performance under the original guaranty, but not from liability for amounts owed prior to the prejudicial alteration. Given Plaintiff’s prompt payment to prevent further loss and the guaranty’s indemnity clause obligating Defendant to indemnify the guarantor for amounts paid to the lender, Defendant is liable to reimburse Plaintiff for the sums Plaintiff paid post-amendment.

Conclusion
Summary judgment is GRANTED in favor of Plaintiff. The Court declares that Plaintiff was discharged from future guaranty obligations following Defendant’s unconsented material modification of the Loan Agreement. Defendant is ORDERED to indemnify Plaintiff for the amounts Plaintiff paid to Lender after the prejudicial alteration, plus costs and pre-judgment interest. Judgment shall be entered accordingly.

This case concerns a dispute arising from a commercial loan made by First Valley Bank to defendant Daniel Mercer, the primary borrower, for the purchase of restaurant equipment. Plaintiff Horizon Capital Partners signed a separate guaranty agreement in connection with the loan and, after Mercer defaulted, paid the remaining balance to the bank. Horizon now seeks reimbursement from Mercer, alleging that as guarantor it became subrogated to the bank’s rights against the borrower.

### Background

In 2021, Mercer executed a promissory note in favor of First Valley Bank. On the same date, Horizon executed a guaranty promising payment if Mercer failed to perform. The note required the bank to provide written notice of default and an opportunity to cure before accelerating the debt. After Mercer missed two monthly payments, the bank did not send the contractually required cure notice. Instead, it negotiated directly with Horizon, accepted payment from Horizon for the accelerated balance, and marked the note “paid in full.” Horizon then filed this action against Mercer seeking the amount it paid, plus fees and interest.

Mercer contends Horizon cannot recover because the bank failed to comply with the note’s notice provisions, and Horizon, standing in the bank’s shoes, acquired no greater rights than the bank possessed.

### Legal Issue

The principal issue is whether a guarantor who satisfies a borrower’s debt after default may recover from the borrower when the lender failed to satisfy a condition precedent to enforcement of the underlying note.

### Applicable Law and Standard

A guarantor who pays a debt may, under principles of equitable subrogation or reimbursement, pursue the principal obligor. But subrogation does not enlarge the guarantor’s rights; the guarantor acquires only those rights the creditor could have enforced. Likewise, where a contract makes notice and opportunity to cure a condition precedent to acceleration or collection, failure to comply bars enforcement unless waived.

### Analysis

The note here expressly required written notice of default and a ten-day cure period before acceleration. The record contains no evidence that the bank provided such notice. Horizon argues Mercer’s payment default alone triggered immediate liability. That position is inconsistent with the note’s plain language. The lender’s right to accelerate was conditional, not automatic.

Because the bank accelerated and collected without satisfying a condition precedent, its claim against Mercer for the accelerated balance was unenforceable at that time. Horizon’s payment to the bank did not cure that defect. A guarantor cannot, by voluntary payment, revive rights the creditor had not properly perfected. Nor has Horizon shown that Mercer waived notice or otherwise consented to immediate acceleration.

Horizon also invokes equitable reimbursement. Equity, however, follows the law. Where the underlying obligation was not enforceable in the manner asserted, equitable relief cannot be used to circumvent the borrower’s contractual defenses.

### Conclusion

Because the lender failed to provide the notice required by the loan documents, Horizon acquired no enforceable right to recover the accelerated balance from Mercer. Judgment is therefore entered **for the defendant, Daniel Mercer**. Plaintiff’s claims are dismissed.

As a condition of the loan, the plaintiff executed a written guaranty promising to answer for the debt if the borrower failed to pay. The note required monthly payments and contained standard default provisions. After several missed payments, the lender declared the loan in default and demanded payment from both the borrower and the guarantor. The plaintiff paid a portion of the outstanding balance under the guaranty and then sued the defendant for reimbursement.

The defendant responded that the lender had materially altered the repayment schedule without the borrower’s consent and had extended additional time for payment, thereby discharging the guarantor’s obligations. The defendant further argued that the plaintiff, having voluntarily paid under a defective guaranty arrangement, could not shift the loss to the borrower.

A guaranty is construed according to ordinary contract principles. A guarantor is generally liable only to the extent of the written undertaking, and material changes to the underlying obligation made without the guarantor’s consent may discharge the guarantor if the changes increase the guarantor’s risk or alter the bargain in a substantial way. In an action for reimbursement or subrogation, the plaintiff bears the burden of proving a valid, enforceable payment made under a continuing obligation.

The record supports the defendant’s position. The lender and borrower amended the repayment terms after the loan was already in default, extending the maturity date and restructuring the payment schedule. The guaranty agreement required the guarantor’s written consent to any material modification affecting the risk assumed. No such consent appears in the record. The plaintiff argues that the changes were merely administrative and did not increase exposure, but the extension of time and revised amortization schedule plainly altered the timing and character of the obligation.

Because the guarantor’s liability was contingent on the original terms of the debt, the unauthorized modification discharged the guaranty. Once discharged, the plaintiff’s payment was not made pursuant to an enforceable continuing guaranty obligation. Without a valid basis for reimbursement, the plaintiff cannot recover from the defendant on the theory asserted.

### Conclusion

The court concludes that the guarantor was discharged by the material, unauthorized modification of the loan agreement. Accordingly, judgment is entered for the defendant.

Plaintiff, an online seller, brought this action seeking a declaration that defendant, a co-seller, was not a partner in plaintiff’s business and therefore had no ownership interest in the proceeds or control over the enterprise. Defendant contends that the parties’ repeated collaboration, shared customer communications, and division of certain profits established an informal partnership.

### Background

The record shows that plaintiff operated an online storefront selling refurbished electronics. Defendant occasionally assisted by listing items, answering customer messages, and packaging shipments. The parties never signed a written agreement. Plaintiff maintained the storefront account, controlled pricing, paid platform fees, and reported the income on plaintiff’s tax filings. Defendant was compensated irregularly from time to time, usually by fixed transfers after busy sales periods. Defendant also used the phrase “our shop” in messages to customers and posted promotional content on social media.

After a dispute arose over inventory and revenue, defendant asserted an ownership interest in the business and demanded access to the storefront account and sales records. Plaintiff denied that any partnership existed and filed suit.

### Legal Issue

The central issue is whether the parties’ conduct created an informal partnership under applicable state law, or whether defendant was merely an independent helper or contractor.

### Applicable Law and Standard of Review

A partnership generally requires an association of two or more persons to carry on as co-owners a business for profit. Courts look to objective indicia of co-ownership, including the right to control the business, sharing of profits and losses, capital contributions, and the parties’ intent as reflected in their conduct. No single factor is dispositive, and labels used informally by the parties do not control if the underlying facts do not support co-ownership.

### Analysis

The evidence does not establish a partnership. Although defendant assisted with sales operations and occasionally received payments tied to business activity, the record shows plaintiff retained exclusive control over the storefront account, pricing, inventory purchases, and tax reporting. Defendant did not contribute startup capital, did not bear losses, and had no authority to bind the business to contracts or expenses. The sporadic transfers to defendant are consistent with compensation for services, not a distribution of partnership profits.

The use of phrases such as “our shop” in casual communications is insufficient to create a partnership absent objective evidence of shared ownership. Likewise, defendant’s promotional efforts and customer interactions show participation in the business, but participation alone does not establish co-ownership. The law requires more than collaboration; it requires an agreement, express or implied, to carry on the enterprise as partners. That showing is missing here.

### Conclusion

Because defendant failed to prove the existence of an informal partnership, plaintiff is entitled to judgment declaring that no partnership existed between the parties. Judgment is entered for plaintiff.

Whether the parties formed an informal partnership under applicable partnership law for the joint sale of goods through online listings, and, if so, whether plaintiff is entitled to relief; if not, whether plaintiff may recover on alternative theories (e.g., unjust enrichment, conversion, accounting).

Formation of a partnership in fact requires evidence of an agreement—express or implied—to carry on a business for profit, with intent to share profits, joint ownership or control over the business, and mutual agency. Acme Digital Goods, LLC, Plaintiff,
v.

Background
Plaintiff Acme Digital Goods, LLC sells consumer electronics through major online marketplaces. Defendant Jordan Perez is an individual seller who, for several months, listed complementary accessories and occasionally fulfilled overflow orders for Acme when Acme’s inventory was constrained. The parties communicated by email and messaging through the marketplace platform. Plaintiff alleges that the parties formed an informal partnership to co-sell branded bundles, entitling Plaintiff to an accounting and a share of Defendant’s profits. Defendant denies any partnership, asserting that, at most, the parties engaged in ad hoc referral and drop-ship arrangements, each retaining separate accounts, inventory, pricing, and risk. Whether the parties formed an informal partnership such that Defendant owes fiduciary duties and is obligated to account to Plaintiff for profits from online sales.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
A partnership is formed when two or more persons associate to carry on as co-owners a business for profit. Factors include: (1) an agreement—express or implied—to share profits and losses; (2) joint control or right of control; (3) contribution of capital or services to a common enterprise; and (4) holding out to third parties as partners. No single factor is dispositive, but profit sharing is strong evidence unless the profits are received as payment for services or goods. The party asserting partnership bears the burden of proof by a preponderance of the evidence.

Analysis
Plaintiff has not demonstrated an agreement to share profits and losses. The record shows that Defendant invoiced Plaintiff on a per-order basis at agreed transfer prices for overflow fulfillment. Payments were characterized as reimbursements for goods and shipping plus a fixed handling fee. Such compensation is consistent with a vendor or independent contractor relationship, not partnership profit sharing. There is no evidence of loss sharing; Defendant bore return and chargeback risks only on orders Defendant fulfilled, and Plaintiff absorbed such risks on its own orders.

As to joint control, each party maintained its own marketplace account, independently set pricing, and managed separate customer communications. Occasional coordination about inventory and product bundling did not amount to a mutual right of control over a single business enterprise.

Regarding contribution to a common venture, the parties did not pool funds or create joint inventory. Cross-listing instances were limited and transactional, with each party shipping from its own stock.

Owner of Goods, Plaintiff,

Opinion and Order

Background
Plaintiff, a wholesaler of electronic components, delivered a palette of microprocessors to Defendant, a contract manufacturer, under a written service agreement for inspection and integration into assembled boards. After inspection, Defendant identified serial-number discrepancies and possible counterfeit indicators on a portion of the lot and, pursuant to the agreement’s quality-control provisions, placed the entire shipment in quarantine pending verification of provenance. Plaintiff demanded immediate return of all components. Defendant declined to release the goods until Plaintiff provided documentation demonstrating chain of custody and manufacturer certifications, or permitted a joint audit. Plaintiff instead filed suit for conversion, alleging that Defendant’s refusal to return the goods upon demand was an unlawful exercise of dominion over Plaintiff’s property. The trial court granted summary judgment to Defendant. Plaintiff appeals.

Issue
Whether Defendant’s refusal to return bailed goods, conditioned on contractual and commercially reasonable verification steps, constitutes conversion.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
Conversion requires an intentional exercise of dominion or control over chattel that seriously interferes with the owner’s rights, such that the actor may justly be required to pay the full value of the chattel. A bailee’s qualified refusal to surrender possession is not conversion if supported by a valid lien, contractual right, or a good-faith, reasonable doubt as to the claimant’s right to possession, and the bailee acts without unreasonable delay. We review the grant of summary judgment de novo, viewing the record in the light most favorable to the nonmovant.

Analysis
The undisputed record shows Plaintiff delivered the goods under a service agreement that (1) authorized Defendant to perform authenticity testing; (2) required quarantine of suspect items; and (3) permitted withholding release pending provision of documentation sufficient to resolve discrepancies. Defendant’s refusal was expressly conditioned on receipt of chain-of-custody and certification documents or a joint audit—conditions tethered to the contract and industry standards addressing counterfeit risks.

Plaintiff argues that any refusal after demand constitutes conversion. That is incorrect. A bailee presented with credible grounds to question the right to immediate possession may assert a qualified refusal without committing conversion, provided the refusal is reasonable in scope and duration. Here, Defendant presented uncontroverted evidence of serial-number anomalies and failed initial authenticity tests. Defendant promptly notified Plaintiff, offered reasonable paths to resolution, and maintained the goods in segregated storage. There is no evidence of sale, use, or misuse of the components, nor of undue delay attributable to Defendant; rather, the stalemate persisted because Plaintiff declined to furnish the requested documentation or permit the audit.

Plaintiff also invokes a common-law presumption that a bailee must return goods on demand. That presumption yields to contrary contractual terms and commercially reasonable protective measures. The parties’ agreement expressly allowed withholding release in the circumstances presented. On this record, no reasonable factfinder could conclude that Defendant’s conduct “seriously interfered” with Plaintiff’s rights in a manner warranting the remedy of conversion.

Conclusion
Because Defendant’s conditional refusal was grounded in contractual authority and commercially reasonable, good-faith concerns, and because Plaintiff failed to meet the conditions for release, the elements of conversion are not satisfied. The judgment of the trial court granting summary judgment to Defendant is affirmed.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
Exculpatory clauses are disfavored and strictly construed against the drafter. They may be enforceable as to ordinary negligence only if they: (1) clearly and unambiguously express the intent to release the defendant from its own negligence; (2) are not contrary to public policy; and (3) are not procedurally or substantively unconscionable. The waiver here contains general language referencing “NEGLIGENCE,” which, if clear and conspicuous, may evidence an intent to release ordinary negligence claims. The record, viewed favorably to Plaintiff, supports a triable claim that the injury resulted from Defendant’s failure to inspect or correctly rig the device—risks not inherent to climbing but stemming from provider negligence in fulfilling safety responsibilities. Background
Plaintiff Emily Smith filed a civil action against Defendant Daniel Johnson, a former acquaintance, alleging that Defendant’s repeated unwanted text messages and social media direct messages over a three-month period caused her emotional distress and other compensable harm. Plaintiff asserted claims for intentional infliction of emotional distress (IIED), intrusion upon seclusion, and negligence. The undisputed record shows Defendant sent approximately 30 messages after Plaintiff ended their acquaintance, including two requests to meet and multiple apologies. Plaintiff did not block Defendant, though she did respond twice instructing him to stop contacting her. There were no threats, in-person encounters, or disclosures of private facts. Plaintiff sought damages for anxiety, sleep disturbance, and time missed from work, but provided no medical records or expert testimony. After discovery, Defendant moved for summary judgment.

Legal Issue
Whether the evidence, viewed in the light most favorable to Plaintiff, creates a triable issue that Defendant’s unwanted contact constitutes (1) extreme and outrageous conduct causing severe emotional distress, (2) a highly offensive intrusion upon seclusion, or (3) negligent conduct causing compensable harm.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
Summary judgment is appropriate where there is no genuine dispute of material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. To establish IIED, a plaintiff must show extreme and outrageous conduct that intentionally or recklessly causes severe emotional distress, typically requiring distress of a nature no reasonable person should be expected to endure. Intrusion upon seclusion requires an intentional intrusion into private affairs that would be highly offensive to a reasonable person. Negligence requires duty, breach, causation, and legally cognizable damages, which for purely emotional injuries normally require proof of severe distress supported by objective evidence.

Analysis
Even crediting Plaintiff’s account, the content and frequency of Defendant’s messages—numerous apologies and requests to talk, devoid of threats, obscenity, or public dissemination—do not rise to the level of extreme and outrageous conduct. Persistent but nonthreatening digital communications, particularly where a recipient retains the ability to block contact, fall short of the high threshold courts impose for IIED. Moreover, Plaintiff offers no medical documentation, diagnosis, or expert testimony to substantiate severe emotional distress.

For intrusion upon seclusion, while repeated contact can be annoying and unwelcome, the tort requires a highly offensive prying into one’s private affairs. Defendant did not obtain or disclose private information, surveil Plaintiff, or physically invade a private space. His direct messages were directed solely to Plaintiff through ordinary communication channels that she could, but did not, block. On these facts, no reasonable jury could find a highly offensive intrusion.

Plaintiff’s negligence claim fails for lack of duty beyond the general obligation to refrain from unreasonable conduct and for lack of cognizable damages. Absent physical impact or independently unlawful conduct, recovery for purely emotional harm demands objective proof of severity and causation, which is not present here. Plaintiff’s missed work and sleep issues, uncorroborated by medical or employer records, are insufficient.

Conclusion
Because no reasonable factfinder could conclude that Defendant’s conduct meets the elements of IIED, intrusion upon seclusion, or negligence, Defendant’s motion for summary judgment is granted. Judgment shall enter for Defendant on all claims. Each party shall bear its own costs.

Questions of contract interpretation and application of common-law principles of contribution are reviewed de novo. Under general contract principles, courts give effect to the plain language of the lease. At common law, co-tenants in possession share obligations connected to the use and preservation of the premises, including necessary expenses incident to occupancy. The lease’s use of “Tenant” is collective, identifying both signatories as tenants jointly responsible for lease obligations. Utilities such as electricity and gas are necessary expenses directly incident to the co-tenants’ joint occupancy and benefit both parties. In the absence of a specific allocation, the equitable default is that each co-tenant bears a proportionate share, typically equal where both held equal possessory rights and simultaneously occupied the premises. Background
Plaintiff, the owner of a commercial storage unit, sues Defendant, who agreed to temporarily hold and monitor Plaintiff’s property while Plaintiff was absent. Plaintiff alleges that Defendant accepted keys and a limited custodial duty, and that during Defendant’s custodial period certain stored items were damaged by water from a malfunctioning heater in Defendant’s care. Plaintiff seeks damages for the loss. Defendant contends it was a gratuitous bailee and denies liability, asserting no negligence and that Plaintiff bore the risk.

Legal Issue
Whether a temporary custodian (defendant) who accepted possession of another’s property owed a duty of care and, if so, whether the custodian’s failure to exercise that duty makes the custodian liable for damage to the property while in custody.

Applicable Law / Standard of Review
When one party voluntarily takes custody of another’s property, the law treats that party as a bailee. A bailee’s duty is determined by the nature of the custody—gratuitous or for compensation—and by any express agreement. A bailee must exercise reasonable care to prevent foreseeable harm and is liable for loss caused by negligent breach of that duty. Summary judgment standards require the court, on undisputed facts, to apply law to those facts; here, the parties’ factual stipulations control.

Analysis
The parties stipulated that Defendant accepted keys and agreed to monitor the storage unit for a specified three-week period without compensation. Acceptance of possession transformed Defendant into a gratuitous bailee. Even a gratuitous bailee owes a duty to exercise reasonable care, particularly to protect against foreseeable risks during custody. Defendant knew or should have known the storage space contained temperature-sensitive materials and that mechanical systems in the unit could pose a risk if not monitored. Plaintiff presented evidence that Defendant failed to inspect the heater or to install a temporary alarm and that Defendant left the unit unattended for multiple consecutive days. The heater subsequently malfunctioned, causing water damage.

Defendant argues lack of compensation reduces the standard of care. While the obligation of a gratuitous bailee may be measured against what is reasonable under the circumstances, it does not absolve the bailee of liability for negligent inattention that substantially increases risk to the property. On the undisputed facts, Defendant’s minimal and sporadic checks were insufficient to discharge the duty to exercise reasonable care. No evidence shows a superseding cause or that Plaintiff assumed the risk; Plaintiff had no reason to anticipate negligent monitoring after expressly entrusting Defendant with custody.

Conclusion
Defendant, as a gratuitous bailee, breached the duty to exercise reasonable care in custody of Plaintiff’s property and is liable for the resulting damage. Judgment is entered in favor of Plaintiff. Damages and costs shall be determined in accordance with the court’s procedures.

Jordan Ellis, Plaintiff,
v.
Morningstar Event Services, LLC, Defendant.

OPINION AND ORDER

Background
Plaintiff Jordan Ellis owns a grand piano, a 1928 Model L, which he loaned to Defendant Morningstar Event Services, LLC for use at a three-day charity gala. The parties executed a written bailment agreement under which Defendant agreed to transport, store, and return the piano in “the same condition as received, ordinary wear excepted.” The agreement required Defendant to keep the instrument in a climate-controlled environment, prohibit public access when unattended, and insure it for loss or damage. Upon return, the piano exhibited a cracked soundboard and multiple case abrasions. Plaintiff’s expert attributed the damage to exposure to heat and low humidity and to impact consistent with unpadded movement. Defendant denied negligence, asserting that the damage was preexisting or the result of latent defects and that it exercised ordinary care.

Legal Issue
The dispositive issue is whether, under a bailment for mutual benefit, Defendant is liable for damage to the bailed property that occurred while in its exclusive custody.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
In a mutual-benefit bailment, delivery of the property in good condition and its return in damaged condition raises a rebuttable presumption of the bailee’s negligence. The bailee bears the burden to come forward with evidence of due care or an alternative, non-negligent cause. Contract terms allocating duties may inform the standard of care. Damages are measured by the reasonable cost of repair or diminution in value.

Analysis
Plaintiff established delivery of the piano in good condition by photographs and a pre-loan inspection checklist signed by both parties. The return inspection, also signed, documents new abrasions and tonal impairment. The temporal proximity and exclusive custody by Defendant for three days are undisputed. Accordingly, the presumption of negligence attaches.

Defendant’s evidence does not rebut that presumption. Its manager testified generally that the piano was stored “indoors,” but offered no humidity or temperature logs despite the contract’s climate-control requirement. The venue’s facilities director testified that the storage room’s HVAC was turned off overnight to reduce noise and that portable dehumidifiers were not used. Defendant also failed to produce the insurance certificate required by the agreement, suggesting lax compliance with contractual safeguards. As to handling, Defendant presented no proof of padding or dollies used during transport beyond conclusory assertions. By contrast, Plaintiff’s expert credibly explained that a rapid humidity drop can cause soundboard cracking and that the surface abrasions are consistent with unpadded movement—mechanisms within Defendant’s control to prevent.

Defendant’s suggestion of a latent defect is speculative. No prior cracking appears in pre-loan records; Plaintiff’s tuner documented stable condition two weeks before delivery. The bailee must do more than posit alternative causes; it must produce evidence of due care or a specific non-negligent cause. It has not.

Plaintiff’s repair estimate, corroborated by a piano restoration specialist, establishes damages of $12,800 for soundboard stabilization and refinishing, plus $1,200 for transport and tuning. These amounts are reasonable and uncontroverted.

Conclusion
Plaintiff has proven a mutual-benefit bailment, delivery in good condition, and return in damaged condition. Defendant failed to rebut the presumption of negligence and breached its contractual duties. Judgment is entered for Plaintiff in the amount of $14,000, plus costs and prejudgment interest as permitted by law.

Does the defendant, as temporary custodian of plaintiff’s shed, face liability for damage discovered during storage when the defendant asserts it exercised reasonable care and the plaintiff cannot show causation or a breach of an express contractual warranty?

This court reviews the trial court’s findings of fact for clear error and legal conclusions de novo. Plaintiff argues defendant stored the shed outdoors on gravel without roofing and therefore allowed water intrusion. Defendant’s yard manager testified to standard practice of elevating small structures off the ground and inspecting for damage on intake; photographic intake records note prior moisture stains along the lower panels. Expert testimony established that water infiltration likely predated custody and could be exacerbated by seasonal humidity.

Plaintiff Creditor brought this action to recover $18,500 allegedly loaned to Defendant Debtor. At trial, Plaintiff introduced a handwritten document signed by Defendant stating: “I owe Creditor $18,500, to be repaid by December 1.” The note was dated and bore Defendant’s signature. Plaintiff testified that the writing was executed on the same day Plaintiff advanced the funds in cash to Defendant for business expenses. Defendant did not dispute the signature, but argued the document was merely a “personal reminder,” not an enforceable promise, and further contended that Plaintiff failed to prove the debt remained unpaid.

The trial court entered judgment for Plaintiff. Defendant appeals, asserting that the handwritten IOU was insufficient as a matter of law to establish an outstanding obligation.

**Legal Issue**

The principal issue is whether a handwritten IOU, authenticated and signed by the debtor, together with supporting testimony, is sufficient to prove the existence of an enforceable unpaid debt.

**Applicable Law and Standard of Review**

A plaintiff seeking recovery on a debt must prove the existence of an obligation, the defendant’s assent to that obligation, and nonpayment. A signed written acknowledgment of indebtedness is generally admissible as evidence of a debt and may constitute a binding promise where its terms reasonably identify the parties, the amount owed, and repayment. Contract formation does not require formal language if the writing objectively manifests an intent to undertake an obligation.

On appeal from a bench trial, factual findings are reviewed for clear error, while legal conclusions are reviewed de novo. The appellate court gives due regard to the trial court’s assessment of witness credibility.

**Analysis**

The handwritten IOU here contains the essential terms of a debt: the identity of the obligee, a sum certain, and a repayment date. Its language—“I owe Creditor $18,500, to be repaid by December 1”—is not equivocal. It is a direct acknowledgment of present indebtedness coupled with a repayment commitment. Courts routinely recognize such writings as competent evidence of a loan obligation, even when informal in form.

Defendant’s argument that the note was merely a reminder is unpersuasive. The objective meaning of the signed writing controls, not a later, self-serving characterization. Defendant admitted signing the document and offered no competing writing, receipt, or other documentary evidence showing a different arrangement. Plaintiff’s testimony that funds were advanced contemporaneously with execution of the note further supports the existence of consideration.

As to nonpayment, Plaintiff testified that no repayment was ever made. Once Plaintiff established the debt through the signed IOU and testimony, the burden of production shifted to Defendant to present some evidence of payment. Defendant produced none—no canceled check, transfer record, receipt, or credible testimony identifying any repayment. The trial court was entitled to credit Plaintiff’s account and reject Defendant’s unsupported denial.

**Conclusion**

The handwritten IOU, authenticated by Defendant’s admitted signature and corroborated by Plaintiff’s testimony, sufficiently proves an enforceable outstanding obligation. The trial court did not err in finding that Defendant owes Plaintiff $18,500. Judgment is therefore **affirmed in favor of Plaintiff Creditor**.

A plaintiff asserting breach of a loan agreement or seeking recovery on a debt bears the burden of proving the existence of an enforceable obligation, the material terms of that obligation, performance by the plaintiff, breach by the defendant, and resulting damages. A signed writing may constitute evidence of indebtedness, but it is not conclusive where material terms are indefinite or where surrounding circumstances create uncertainty as to consideration, payment, or discharge. In a bench trial, the Court weighs credibility and determines whether the evidence establishes liability by a preponderance of the evidence.

The handwritten note has some probative value, but it is insufficient on this record to establish an outstanding obligation. First, the document is materially incomplete. It does not identify when funds were advanced, whether they were in fact advanced, when repayment was due, or whether any later payments or offsets occurred. On claims of tortious interference with contractual relations, a plaintiff must establish (1) the existence of a valid contract, (2) the interferer’s knowledge of the contract, (3) intentional and improper interference inducing or causing a breach, (4) resulting breach, and (5) damages. IN THE SUPERIOR COURT OF HAWTHORNE COUNTY

Acme Design, LLC, Plaintiff,
v.
Northstar Consulting Group, Inc., Defendant.

Opinion and Order

Background
Acme Design, LLC (Acme), a commercial interior design firm, entered into a written contract with Beacon Realty Partners (Beacon) to design and oversee the build-out of Beacon’s new office space. The agreement provided for staged payments and a termination clause requiring written notice and an opportunity to cure any alleged default. After work commenced, Northstar Consulting Group, Inc. (Northstar), a competitor engaged by Beacon to advise on project costs, sent Beacon several emails asserting that Acme lacked the required professional licensure for commercial projects and had been sanctioned by state regulators. Beacon, relying on Northstar’s communications, terminated the contract without providing the contractual cure period and engaged a different firm. Acme sued Northstar for tortious interference with contract, seeking lost profits. The case was tried to the court on a stipulated record.

Legal Issue
Whether Northstar, by communicating false statements to Beacon, intentionally and improperly induced Beacon’s breach of its contract with Acme, thereby causing Acme damages.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
To establish tortious interference with contract, a plaintiff must show: (1) the existence of a valid and enforceable contract, (2) defendant’s knowledge of the contract, (3) intentional and improper interference inducing or causing a breach, and (4) resultant damages. Truthful, good-faith advice may be privileged; however, knowingly false statements or reckless disregard for truth are improper. The plaintiff bears the burden by a preponderance of the evidence.

Analysis
The first two elements are uncontested. The written agreement between Acme and Beacon is valid and enforceable, and Northstar’s engagement letter and internal correspondence acknowledge the contract and its terms.

As to interference, the record shows that Northstar’s principal told Beacon that Acme lacked required licensure and had been sanctioned. State licensing records submitted by stipulation establish that Acme held a current commercial design registration and had no disciplinary history. Northstar’s claim that it relied on an “industry bulletin” is unsupported; no such bulletin was produced, and Northstar conceded it conducted no verification through the state registry, a public and readily accessible source. The court finds Northstar’s statements were false and made, at minimum, with reckless disregard for their truth.

Causation is also established. Beacon’s termination notice cites Northstar’s emails as the basis for immediate termination, notwithstanding the contract’s cure provision. Beacon’s project manager testified that, but for the licensure and sanctions concerns raised by Northstar, Beacon would have afforded Acme the contractual cure opportunity and continued performance. The immediate switch to a replacement firm confirms that Northstar’s communications induced the breach.

Finally, damages were proven with reasonable certainty. Acme presented the remaining contract balance and anticipated profit on the unperformed phases, corroborated by contemporaneous budgets and prior phase margins. Northstar’s argument that Beacon invoked a contractual right to terminate fails; while termination was permitted, the contract required written notice and a cure period absent an emergency. Beacon’s failure to follow that procedure, precipitated by Northstar’s false statements, constitutes a breach proximately caused by Northstar.

Conclusion
Acme has proven each element of tortious interference with contract. Judgment is entered for Acme Design, LLC. The court awards lost profits in the amount of $184,500, plus prejudgment interest as permitted by statute, and reasonable costs. Northstar’s affirmative defenses based on privilege and good-faith advice are rejected. A separate order regarding interest calculation and costs will issue.

**Background**

Plaintiff Meridian Components, Inc. entered into a two-year supply agreement with North Valley Fabrication, LLC for the purchase of specialty steel housings used in industrial pumps. Several months into the contract, North Valley terminated the agreement, citing concerns about Meridian’s financial stability and alleged regulatory noncompliance. Meridian then filed this action against defendant Apex Market Analytics, a consulting firm retained by North Valley, alleging tortious interference with contract. Meridian contends Apex supplied false information to North Valley—specifically, that Meridian was under imminent enforcement action and unable to meet future production obligations—and that this misinformation induced North Valley’s breach.

Following discovery, Apex moved for summary judgment. The record includes internal emails, a written risk memorandum prepared by Apex, deposition testimony from North Valley’s procurement director, and evidence concerning Meridian’s production delays and outstanding tax liens.

**Legal Issue**

The principal issue is whether Meridian has produced sufficient evidence that Apex intentionally and improperly induced North Valley to breach the supply agreement by providing false information, rather than merely furnishing an assessment that North Valley independently relied upon in deciding to terminate.

**Applicable Law and Standard of Review**

To prevail on a claim for tortious interference with contract, a plaintiff generally must prove: (1) a valid contract; (2) defendant’s knowledge of that contract; (3) intentional procurement of its breach; (4) use of improper means or an improper purpose; and (5) resulting damages. Where the alleged improper means is false information, the plaintiff must show the statements were materially false, made without privilege or justification, and were a substantial factor in causing the breach. On summary judgment, the court views the evidence in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party, but conclusory assertions and speculation do not create a triable issue.

**Analysis**

Meridian has established the existence of a contract and Apex’s awareness of it. The claim fails, however, on falsity, intent, and causation.

First, the challenged statements are not shown to be materially false in the relevant sense. Apex’s memorandum described Meridian as presenting “heightened counterparty risk,” referenced public tax filings, noted recent shipment delays, and stated that “regulatory exposure appears possible” based on customer complaints and incomplete certification records. Those are evaluative judgments grounded in disclosed facts, not demonstrably false statements of existing fact. Although one email used the phrase “imminent enforcement action,” the undisputed testimony shows Apex relayed an unconfirmed industry report and expressly advised North Valley to verify it independently.

Second, the record does not support a finding that Apex acted with the purpose of inducing breach. Apex was engaged to provide risk analysis, and there is no evidence it stood to benefit from termination or harbored animus toward Meridian.

Third, North Valley’s decision was not shown to have been caused principally by Apex’s report. Its procurement director testified that termination followed Meridian’s repeated late deliveries, refusal to provide updated financial assurances, and North Valley’s own review of public lien records. Independent business reasons defeat the required showing that Apex’s statements were the substantial factor producing the breach.

**Conclusion**

Because Meridian has not produced evidence from which a reasonable factfinder could conclude that Apex used materially false information or improper means to induce breach, defendant’s motion for summary judgment is **GRANTED**. Judgment shall be entered in favor of Apex Market Analytics.

Whether the handwritten agreement between Homeowner and Contractor constituted an enforceable contract for home repairs.

On a motion to dismiss, courts accept well-pleaded factual allegations as true. On summary judgment, the movant must show there is no genuine dispute of material fact and is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Contract enforceability requires offer, acceptance, consideration, and sufficient definiteness of material terms. The statute of frauds requires certain contracts to be in writing signed by the party to be charged, but services to be performed within one year and contracts for the sale of goods over a price threshold may vary by jurisdiction; repairs to a specific home are typically not within the statute of frauds if performance is to be completed within a year and the agreement is in writing signed by the party sought to be charged.

The handwritten note, signed by both parties, lists the scope (roof replacement, gutter repair, repaint exterior trim), the total price of $7,500, and payment terms (two installments). Whether the handwritten document created an enforceable contract for home repairs.

Applicable Law and Standard of Review
To be enforceable, a contract requires mutual assent and reasonably certain terms sufficient to determine the existence of a breach and provide an appropriate remedy. Essential terms for construction agreements typically include scope of work, price or a method for determining price, materials, start and completion dates or a reasonable timeframe, and any contingencies. Where parties contemplate a later formal writing or condition performance on events that have not occurred, preliminary writings may be nonbinding unless the parties clearly manifest an intent to be bound immediately. On summary judgment, the movant must show no genuine dispute of material fact and entitlement to judgment as a matter of law. Ambiguities are construed in favor of the nonmovant, but indefiniteness is a question of law when essential terms are missing.

Analysis
The handwritten document identifies a general subject—“exterior siding replacement and porch repairs”—but omits material specifics. It references “materials TBD,” provides only an “approx. $8,000” price, and ties commencement to “spring after permits,” without identifying who would obtain permits, what governing specifications apply, or a definite start or completion date. The notation “50% start/50% finish” presupposes a binding contract but does not cure the uncertainty regarding total cost or scope.

The record also reflects that both parties contemplated further steps before being bound. The writing references permits and lender approval, neither of which had been obtained. Emails submitted by Plaintiff indicate she asked Defendant to “send over the formal contract once you finalize materials,” to which Defendant replied that he would do so after supplier quotes. This demonstrates contemplation of a later, more definite agreement. Unlike cases where market indices or unit prices supply a method to determine consideration, this writing offers no workable mechanism for a court to compute damages without impermissible speculation.

Plaintiff argues that customary practices and reasonableness could fill gaps. While courts may imply incidental terms, they do not supply essential terms where the record shows the parties had not reached agreement on them. Here, the contingencies and open material terms render the writing an unenforceable preliminary understanding.

Because the handwritten document lacks essential terms and evidences an intent to finalize agreement only after permits, material selections, and a formal contract, no enforceable contract was formed as a matter of law. Plaintiff Homeowner filed this action seeking recovery for unpaid repairs performed at Plaintiff’s residence. The parties agree that Contractor visited Plaintiff’s property, made minor repairs, and that Plaintiff provided a handwritten note memorializing terms. Plaintiff contends the handwritten note constitutes a definitive contract obligating Contractor to perform additional work and to accept payment on the terms stated; Plaintiff seeks damages for alleged breach when Contractor stopped work and refused to complete the additional tasks. Contractor moves for judgment on the pleadings, asserting the handwritten note is unenforceable for lack of clear mutual assent, fails the statute of frauds where applicable, and that no meeting of the minds occurred.

Legal Issue
Whether the handwritten agreement between Homeowner and Contractor created an enforceable contract obligating Contractor to perform the contested repairs.

Standard of Review
On a motion for judgment on the pleadings, the court accepts the complaint’s factual allegations as true and determines whether those facts state a plausible claim for relief. Contract formation requires mutual assent to definite terms and, for certain construction-related agreements, compliance with any applicable statute of frauds.

Applicable Law
Under general contract principles, an enforceable contract requires offer, acceptance, consideration, and sufficiently definite terms. The statute of frauds may require written evidence of agreements that cannot be performed within one year or involve real property, and some jurisdictions require written contracts for certain home improvement agreements exceeding a specified dollar amount.

Analysis
The handwritten note here is ambiguous in crucial respects. It lists several tasks (e.g., "fix porch, paint, replace railing") with a scribbled total and the date, but contains no clear indication of price allocation per task, no express acceptance or signature by Contractor, and no schedule for completion. Plaintiff admits the note was prepared by Plaintiff and given to Contractor during a single site visit. Contractor verbally acknowledged willingness to inspect and provide a formal estimate. Plaintiff’s complaint does not allege that Contractor signed the note or that the parties agreed on a final price or timeline.

Under established principles, a unilateral memorandum prepared by one party does not establish a binding contract absent corroboration by the other party demonstrating assent to the specific terms. Moreover, where home improvement contracts exceed statutory thresholds or involve alterations to a fixed structure, many statutes require written, signed agreements setting forth essential terms; the complaint does not allege compliance with any such formalities. Even assuming some repair work was performed, quantum meruit may permit recovery for reasonable value of services rendered, but Plaintiff seeks enforcement of the handwritten note as a contract and damages for incomplete additional work, which requires proof of mutual assent to concrete terms.

Conclusion
Because Plaintiff fails to allege facts demonstrating a meeting of the minds, a signed writing by both parties, or compliance with applicable formal requirements for home improvement contracts, the handwritten note is not an enforceable contract as pleaded. Defendant’s motion for judgment on the pleadings is GRANTED. Plaintiff’s claim for breach of contract is dismissed without prejudice to amendment to plead facts demonstrating assent or statutory compliance. Judgment for Defendant.

A plaintiff seeking to enforce a loan agreement must prove the existence of the contract, the defendant’s obligation, and nonpayment. In evaluating the evidence, the Court applies the preponderance-of-the-evidence standard.

The record supports Lender’s position. First, the agreement unambiguously required payment in cleared funds received by the due date. The central issue is whether Borrower’s disputed $5,000 payment discharged the remaining debt under the loan agreement.

A loan agreement is enforced according to ordinary principles of contract law. Where contract terms are unambiguous, the court gives effect to their plain meaning. Payment discharges a debt only when made in the amount and manner required by the agreement, or when the creditor clearly assents to an alternative performance. An accord and satisfaction requires a bona fide dispute, a tender in full settlement, and knowing acceptance by the creditor.

Because this matter was tried to the court, factual findings are based on the preponderance of the evidence.

**Analysis**

The written loan agreement is clear. It specifies the repayment schedule and requires written approval for any deviation in payment method or terms. Borrower offered no evidence of any written modification reducing the final amount due. Lender introduced the payment ledger and amortization summary, both showing an unpaid balance of $6,875 as of February 20, 2024. Borrower did not meaningfully rebut those records.

Nor did Borrower establish accord and satisfaction. Although the cashier’s check bore the notation “loan paid in full,” that notation alone is insufficient.
