Background

This case arises from a personal loan between plaintiff Lender and defendant Borrower. In a written loan agreement, Lender advanced $25,000 to Borrower on January 10, 2023, with repayment in monthly installments and a final balloon payment due December 31, 2023. The agreement specified that payments must be made by bank transfer to Lender’s designated account and that any payment presented as “full satisfaction” must be expressly accepted in writing by Lender. On December 29, 2023, Borrower initiated a bank transfer of $25,000 to Lender but annotated the transfer with the words “Paid in full” and provided an accompanying email stating the transfer was intended to satisfy the debt in full. Lender’s bank received the funds on December 30, 2023; the funds were credited to Lender’s account. Lender did not return the funds, did not provide a written acceptance of “paid in full,” and sued in state court on January 15, 2024, seeking a judgment for an additional $2,500 in late fees and interest that Lender claimed accrued under the contract.

Legal issue

Whether the payment constituting the disputed bank transfer, accompanied by Borrower’s “Paid in full” notation and email, satisfied the loan in full so as to preclude Lender’s claim for additional fees and interest.

Standard of review and applicable law

Contract interpretation and satisfaction of payment are questions of law reviewed de novo. Governing principles include the objective theory of contracts: mutual assent is judged by outward manifestations, and acceptance of a tendered performance is necessary where a tender is conditioned. Additionally, the doctrine of accord and satisfaction applies where a debtor offers a payment in full satisfaction and the creditor accepts it, or where the creditor’s conduct leads a reasonable debtor to believe acceptance occurred. UCC principles regarding negotiable instruments and finality of payment by bank transfer are also relevant; payment by transfer generally discharges the obligor when the creditor receives and applies funds, absent timely objection.

Analysis

Borrower indisputably transferred $25,000 to Lender’s designated account before the due date, and Lender’s bank credited the funds. The dispute hinges on whether Borrower’s “Paid in full” notation and accompanying email constituted an offer of payment in full satisfaction and whether Lender’s conduct amounted to acceptance.

Under the objective standard, Borrower’s notation and explicit email communicated a clear intent that the transferred sum was tendered as full satisfaction. Lender’s silence in response, combined with retention and application of the funds to its account, constitutes conduct reasonably interpreted by Borrower as acceptance. Lender’s failure to return the funds promptly or to provide the written rejection required by the parties’ contract renders its later assertion of additional fees inconsistent with the doctrine of accord and satisfaction. Where a creditor receives a conditional tender and treats the funds as its own without timely rejection, courts frequently hold the creditor has accepted the terms accompanying the payment. Absent evidence that Lender promptly and clearly rejected the conditional nature of the payment before applying it, Lender may not now assert a claim for further amounts.

Conclusion

For the foregoing reasons, judgment is entered for defendant Borrower. The December 29, 2023 payment, accompanied by a clear “Paid in full” communication and retained by Lender without timely rejection, constituted payment in full of the loan obligation. Lender’s claim for additional fees and interest is dismissed. Each party shall bear its own costs.

The central issue is whether Borrower’s disputed payment satisfied the remaining obligation under the loan agreement.

A plaintiff asserting breach of contract must prove the existence of a contract, performance by the plaintiff, breach by the defendant, and resulting damages. Payment is an affirmative defense, and the defendant bears the burden of showing that payment was made and accepted in accordance with the parties’ agreement or subsequent mutual understanding. In interpreting contracts, courts give effect to the parties’ objective manifestations and course of performance. Where a creditor accepts a payment tendered as full satisfaction of a liquidated or readily calculable debt, the creditor may not later disregard that payment absent timely rejection, refund, or proof that the tender was materially defective.

**Analysis**

Borrower met the burden of proving payment. The evidence shows that Lender provided a payoff figure immediately before the transfer, that Borrower remitted that amount to the designated account, and that Lender retained the funds without objection for several weeks before filing suit. The memo notation does not alter that conclusion. Payment instructions in the loan agreement did not require any particular memo language, and Lender’s own records show prior payments were credited despite inconsistent descriptions.

Nor did Lender establish any remaining deficiency. The claimed shortfall rests on late fees and additional interest not reflected in the payoff amount Lender communicated. A creditor who quotes a payoff figure and accepts that amount cannot later impose uncommunicated charges inconsistent with the parties’ contemporaneous exchange. The objective evidence demonstrates mutual assent that the May 28 payment would retire the debt.

**Conclusion**

Because Borrower proved that the disputed payment satisfied the loan under the parties’ agreement and course of dealing, Plaintiff Lender has not established breach. Judgment is entered in favor of Defendant Borrower. Plaintiff’s claims are dismissed with prejudice.
